title: SQL Server batch returns a 0 × 0 data frame when an intermediate aggregate generates a warning
description:
A SQL Server batch returns a 0-row, 0-column data frame through dbGetQuery(), although its final SELECT returns data in SSMS. The batch generates:
```Warning: Null value is eliminated by an aggregate or other SET operation.```
The synthetic example below reproduces this despite SET NOCOUNT ON. Default execution and immediate = TRUE return 0 × 0; immediate = FALSE returns the expected 4 × 5 result.
Expected: retrieve the final SELECT’s result despite the intermediate warning.
This may be related to #573 and #173.


```r
library(DBI)
library(odbc)

connect <- function() {
  dbConnect(odbc(), dsn = "YOUR_DSN")
}

sql <- "
SET ANSI_WARNINGS ON;
SET NOCOUNT ON;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #ExampleEnrolments;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #ExampleIndex;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #ExampleCampus;

SELECT school_id, campus_id, calendar_year, enrolments
INTO #ExampleEnrolments
FROM (VALUES
    (101, 1, 2023, 120),
    (101, 1, 2023, NULL),
    (101, 2, 2023, 90),
    (102, 1, 2024, 80),
    (103, 1, 2024, 60)
) v(school_id, campus_id, calendar_year, enrolments);

SELECT school_id, campus_id, census_year,
       CAST(band AS varchar(255)) AS index_band,
       CAST(index_value AS decimal(6,4)) AS index_value
INTO #ExampleIndex
FROM (VALUES
    (101, 1, 2023, 'Low',    0.1250),
    (101, 2, 2023, 'Medium', 0.4500),
    (102, 1, 2024, 'High',   0.8500)
) v(school_id, campus_id, census_year, band, index_value);

-- SUM encounters NULL and generates the aggregate warning.
SELECT school_id, campus_id, calendar_year,
       SUM(enrolments) AS enrolments
INTO #ExampleCampus
FROM #ExampleEnrolments
GROUP BY school_id, campus_id, calendar_year;

SELECT DISTINCT
    c.school_id,
    c.campus_id,
    c.calendar_year,
    i.index_band,
    i.index_value
FROM #ExampleCampus AS c
LEFT JOIN #ExampleIndex AS i
    ON c.school_id = i.school_id
   AND c.campus_id = i.campus_id
   AND c.calendar_year = i.census_year
ORDER BY c.school_id, c.campus_id, c.calendar_year;
"

# Every test uses a fresh connection.
run_query <- function(query, ...) {
  con <- connect()
  on.exit(dbDisconnect(con))
  dbGetQuery(con, query, ...)
}

# Compare execution modes.
dim(run_query(sql))
dim(run_query(sql, immediate = TRUE))
dim(run_query(sql, immediate = FALSE))
```

```r
> dim(run_query(sql))
[1] 0 0
> dim(run_query(sql, immediate = TRUE))
[1] 0 0
> dim(run_query(sql, immediate = FALSE))
[1] 4 5
```



Tested on Windows with R 4.6.1, DBI 1.3.0, odbc 1.7.2 and Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server.

title: `dbGetRowsAffected()` returns an uninitialized value for statements with no row count (psqlODBC)
description:
With the PostgreSQL ODBC driver, `dbExecute()` on a statement that has no row
count (`SET`, `BEGIN`, `ROLLBACK`, `DROP TABLE`, ...) returns a large meaningless
number instead of 0.

## Reprex

```r
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), driver = "PostgreSQL", server = "127.0.0.1",
                 port = 5432, uid = "postgres", pwd = "...", database = "postgres")
for (s in c("set lock_timeout = 0", "begin", "rollback",
            "create temp table zz_rc (id int)", "insert into zz_rc values (1),(2)",
            "drop table zz_rc")) {
  cat(sprintf("%-36s -> %s\n", s, format(dbExecute(con, s))))
}
#> set lock_timeout = 0                 -> 24559652
#> begin                                -> 24559652
#> rollback                             -> 24559652
#> create temp table zz_rc (id int)     -> 0
#> insert into zz_rc values (1),(2)     -> 2
#> drop table zz_rc                     -> 24559652
dbGetInfo(con)[c("drivername", "driver.version", "db.version")]
#> psqlodbca.so / 18.00.0005 / 16.14 (PostgreSQL 16 in docker)
packageVersion("odbc")
#> 1.7.2  (CRAN, macOS arm64, R 4.5.2; also reproduced with the current main)
```

The number varies between sessions and statements but is stable within one
session, which is what an uninitialized stack variable looks like.

## Cause

`src/nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp`, `statement::statement_impl::affected_rows()`:

```cpp
long affected_rows() const
{
    SQLLEN rows;
    RETCODE rc;
    NANODBC_CALL_RC(SQLRowCount, rc, stmt_, &rows);
    if (!success(rc))
        NANODBC_THROW_DATABASE_ERROR(stmt_, SQL_HANDLE_STMT);
    ...
    return static_cast<long>(rows);
}
```

`rows` is never initialized. The ODBC spec says `SQLRowCount` sets
`*RowCountPtr` to -1 when the count is not available, but psqlODBC returns
`SQL_SUCCESS` without writing it for some statements (it does write 0 for
`CREATE TABLE`, which is why that one looks fine above). `result_rows_affected()`
in `src/result.cpp` already maps negative values to 0, so a -1 would have been
handled; the uninitialized value is positive garbage and passes through.

This is probably also why `test-driver-postgres.R` skips DBItest's
`rows_affected_statement` and `rows_affected_query` with a TODO. The same line
exists in upstream nanodbc (`nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp`, `affected_rows()`), so the fix
belongs there too; reporting here because this is where it bit me (through
`DBI::dbExecute()` in a package that runs `SET` and DDL through it).

## Fix

Assuming we can't get a "real" number, at least initialize to the ODBC "not available" value:

```cpp
SQLLEN rows = -1;
```

With that, the reprex returns 0 for every statement without a count and the
real counts (2 for the `INSERT`) are unchanged. PR to follow.

title: integer64 columns are created as 32-bit INTEGER on PostgreSQL, MySQL, and other backends
description:
`odbcDataType()` maps `integer64` to the 32-bit `INTEGER`/`INT` type on most backends, so `dbCreateTable()` followed by
  `dbAppendTable()` fails for values above 2,147,483,647. Since `dbConnect()` reads `BIGINT` columns as `integer64` by
  default, this affects data read from the database itself.

Fix would be trivial unless this was intentional.

title: Implement the `db*Arrow()` generics
description:
The default fallback implementation in DBI goes from R back to Arrow. Going straight to Arrow would lead to better results if the desired output is actually Arrow/Parquet, among other things.

Documentation for the generics: <https://dbi.r-dbi.org/reference/index.html#arrow>.

Draft implementation, not reviewed manually: <https://github.com/krlmlr/odbc/pull/21>. Let me know how I can further support this.

I'm going in a similar direction with RSQLite/RMariaDB/RPostgres.

title: `BINARY` columns silently truncated to `n mod 1024` bytes (Databricks/Spark ODBC; `pyodbc` unaffected)
description:
## What happens

Reading a `BINARY` column over the Databricks ODBC driver returns fewer bytes than the column holds, with no warning, no error and no truncation indicator. The number of bytes returned is not a cap: it is the true length modulo 1,024.

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::databricks(), httpPath = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_PATH"))

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT cast(repeat('x', 1024) as binary) AS b")$b[[1]] |> length()
#> 1024        # correct

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT cast(repeat('x', 1025) as binary) AS b")$b[[1]] |> length()
#> 1           # one byte returned out of 1,025

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT cast(repeat('x', 5000) as binary) AS b")$b[[1]] |> length()
#> 904
```

A 1,025-byte value comes back as a single byte. Nothing in the result indicates that 1,024 bytes are missing.

## The length follows an exact rule

```
bytes returned = n mod 1024        (with 0 mapping to 1024)
```

This holds for every size tested, with no deviation:

| asked | returned | `n mod 1024` |
|---|---|---|
| 1,024 | 1,024 | 0 → 1,024 |
| 1,025 | 1 | 1 |
| 1,026 | 2 | 2 |
| 1,030 | 6 | 6 |
| 1,050 | 26 | 26 |
| 1,100 | 76 | 76 |
| 1,200 | 176 | 176 |
| 1,500 | 476 | 476 |
| 2,000 | 976 | 976 |
| 2,048 | 1,024 | 0 → 1,024 |
| 2,500 | 452 | 452 |
| 3,000 | 952 | 952 |
| 5,000 | 904 | 904 |
| 10,000 | 784 | 784 |
| 20,000 | 544 | 544 |
| 30,000 | 304 | 304 |
| 42,000 | 16 | 16 |

Two consequences worth drawing out. A payload of exactly *k* × 1,024 bytes comes back intact, so a spot check at 1 KiB, 2 KiB or 4 KiB passes while values just above those boundaries are destroyed. And the damage is not proportional to size: 1,025 bytes loses 99.9% of the value, while 2,048 loses nothing.

The exact modulo, and the fact that multiples of 1,024 survive, is consistent with a length counter wrapping in a 1,024-byte buffer. That is an inference from black-box behaviour; I have not inspected driver internals. Combined with the `pyodbc` result below, the counter is most likely on the `odbc` side rather than in the driver.

## The bytes returned are correct as far as they go

The returned bytes are a byte-exact prefix of the true value, so this is truncation rather than corruption.

This needs testing with a non-uniform payload to mean anything: with `repeat('x', n)` every byte is identical, so *any* truncation trivially looks like a clean prefix. Repeating it with a payload whose bytes all differ (5,120 bytes cycling `00..ff` twenty times):

```r
q <- paste("SELECT unhex(repeat(concat_ws('',",
           "transform(sequence(0,255), i -> lpad(hex(i),2,'0'))), 20)) AS b")
v <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, q)$b[[1]]
length(v)
#> 1024                      # 5,120 mod 1024 == 0, so 1,024
identical(v, as.raw(rep(0:255, 20))[seq_along(v)])
#> TRUE                      # byte-exact prefix of the true value
```

So a byte-count check against the known true length *is* enough to detect this, which is worth stating because it makes a workaround possible for callers who know the expected length.

## No connection-string setting tried changes it

`DefaultBinaryColumnLength` was swept at `2000L`, `8000L`, `65535L` and the string `"100000"`. All four connect successfully and all four return the identical wrong lengths (2,000 → 976, 5,000 → 904, 20,000 → 544).

Integer and string literals were used deliberately. On `odbc` 1.7.0, `build_connection_string()` renders round numbers like `100000` in scientific notation as `1e+05`, which the driver silently ignores; that is [r-dbi/odbc#934](https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/issues/934), fixed by #1016 but not in the current CRAN release. So a naive sweep can look like "the setting has no effect" when the setting never reached the driver. It did here.

Unlike the STRING defect below, I found no client-side setting that fixes this.

## The same bytes arrive intact as `hex()` STRING

This is the sharpest result I have, and it narrows the problem considerably. On the same driver and the same connection, asking for `hex(col)` instead of the `BINARY` column returns the whole payload:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::databricks(),
  httpPath = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_PATH"),
  DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535
)

n <- 1025
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("SELECT cast(repeat('x', %d) as binary) AS b", n))$b[[1]] |> length()
#> 1
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("SELECT hex(cast(repeat('x', %d) as binary)) AS h", n))$h |> nchar()
#> 2050        # 1,025 bytes, complete
```

| asked | as `BINARY` | as `hex()` STRING |
|---|---|---|
| 1,024 | 1,024 | 1,024 |
| 1,025 | **1** | 1,025 |
| 2,000 | **976** | 2,000 |
| 5,000 | **904** | 5,000 |
| 20,000 | **544** | 20,000 |

So neither the driver nor the transport is unable to carry the payload. The loss is specific to the `BINARY` type path.

This also gives callers a workaround that stays on ODBC: select `hex(col)` and decode client-side, at the cost of doubling the bytes on the wire.

```r
h <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT hex(geom) AS h FROM tbl")$h
raw_val <- as.raw(strtoi(substring(h, seq(1, nchar(h), 2), seq(2, nchar(h), 2)), 16L))
```

## `pyodbc` is unaffected, which points at `odbc` rather than the driver

This is the part that identifies the owner. Same driver `.so`, same connection string, same warehouse, minutes apart:

| asked | R, `odbc` 1.7.0 | Python, `pyodbc` 5.3.0 |
|---|---|---|
| 512 | 512 | 512 |
| 1,024 | 1,024 | 1,024 |
| 1,025 | **1** | 1,025 |
| 1,500 | **476** | 1,500 |
| 2,000 | **976** | 2,000 |
| 2,048 | 1,024 | 2,048 |
| 5,000 | **904** | 5,000 |
| 20,000 | **544** | 20,000 |
| 42,000 | **16** | 42,000 |

On a real persisted Delta table with a WKB `BINARY` column, read from storage rather than computed:

| server `length()` | R got | Python got |
|---|---|---|
| 1,046 | **22** | 1,046 |
| 1,062 | **38** | 1,062 |
| 1,078 | **54** | 1,078 |

The Python side used the same driver path (`libsparkodbc_sb64.so`), and `SQLGetInfo` reports the identical driver name and version `2.7.7.1016` on both sides.

I also ran R through raw `odbc::odbc()` with the byte-identical connection string `pyodbc` used, bypassing the `odbc::databricks()` helper entirely:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), .connection_string = cs)  # same string pyodbc used
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT cast(repeat('x', 1025) as binary) AS b")$b[[1]] |> length()
#> 1
```

Same loss. So neither the `databricks()` helper nor any connection-string difference explains it, which is what leads me to `SQL_C_BINARY` buffer handling in `odbc` itself.

## No table is involved

Worth stating because it makes this cheap to reproduce: the ladder above uses no table at all. `cast(repeat('x', n) as binary)` is a scalar expression evaluated by the warehouse, so no catalog, schema, table or Delta property is in play. One line reproduces it:

```r
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT cast(repeat('x', 1025) as binary) AS b")$b[[1]] |> length()
#> 1        # expected 1025
```

The real-table rows above confirm it also happens on data read from storage, but the table is not the variable.

## Relationship to the STRING truncation

STRING columns are also truncated, at 1,023 characters, filed separately as [r-dbi/odbc#1023](https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/issues/1023). That one looks genuinely like a driver default: it is fixable from R with `DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535`, and it truncates to a fixed length rather than a modulo. This one behaves differently and `pyodbc` is unaffected, so I do not assume a common cause. Flagging the pair in case the buffer-length handling turns out to be related.

## The data is intact server-side

`brickster::DatabricksSQL()`, which uses the SQL Statement Execution API and decodes Arrow rather than going over the Thrift/ODBC wire format, returns the same columns byte-exact from the same warehouse in the same session:

| asked | ODBC | `DatabricksSQL()` |
|---|---|---|
| 1,024 | 1,024 | 1,024 |
| 2,000 | **976** | 2,000 |
| 5,000 | **904** | 5,000 |
| 20,000 | **544** | 20,000 |

So the column is stored correctly and at least one client retrieves it correctly. This is a driver/transport issue, not bad data.

## Why the silence is the problem

The practical impact is that WKB geometry in a `BINARY` column cannot be read over this driver. A truncated WKB blob either fails to parse, or parses into a smaller valid geometry, and neither outcome mentions the driver. Any binary payload has the same exposure: serialised model objects, compressed blobs, hashes, images.

Because there is no warning and no indicator, the failure surfaces far from its cause. A hash comparison fails, a blob will not decompress, a geometry is silently the wrong shape. Given that multiples of 1,024 pass cleanly, a smoke test can easily be built out of exactly the sizes that work.

## Environment

```
R           4.5.2 (2025-10-31)
odbc        1.7.0
DBI         1.3.0
brickster   0.2.14
driver      RStudio Spark ODBC Driver 2.7.7.1016 (libsparkodbc_sb64.so)
DBSQL       2026.20
dbms        hive_metastore 3.1.1
compute     serverless SQL warehouse
```

## What I have not established

- Only `DefaultBinaryColumnLength` was swept. Other driver options may affect this, so "no setting fixes it" is not established: only that no setting I tried did.
- One warehouse, one driver version, one DBSQL version, one `R`/`odbc` pair. Nothing here says anything about other versions.
- Serverless SQL warehouse only. No all-purpose cluster or DBR path tested.
- No payload above 42,000 bytes, and only synthetic payloads: no test against a real WKB geometry column.
- The buffer-wrap reading is inferred from returned lengths, not confirmed against driver source or driver logs.
- **Which `odbc` code path is at fault.** The `pyodbc` comparison narrows it to the client, but I have not read `odbc`'s source or built it with instrumentation, so I cannot point at a specific buffer or `SQLGetData` call. `isql` was tried first and cannot help: it truncates its own binary display at a fixed width.
- **Whether this affects other backends.** Only tested against the Databricks/Spark ODBC driver. If the fault is in generic `SQL_C_BINARY` handling, other drivers with large `BINARY` columns may be affected too, and that is untested.

---

## Note for the Databricks/Simba side

Kept short deliberately: on this evidence there is nothing for Simba to fix. `pyodbc` reads the same `BINARY` columns intact through their driver, so the driver moves the bytes correctly. If anything is worth passing on, it is only that the R client has a `BINARY` buffer bug against their driver, in case they field a report about it from another direction.

title: `odbc::databricks()` fails to auto-detect driver on Windows when registered as "Databricks ODBC Driver"
description:
`odbc::databricks()`'s auto-detection logic (`databricks_default_driver()` in `R/driver-databricks.R`) hardcodes the Windows fallback driver name as `"Databricks"`:

```r
find_default_driver(
  databricks_default_driver_paths(),
  fallbacks = c("Databricks", "Simba Spark ODBC Driver"),
  label = "Databricks/Spark",
  call = quote(DBI::dbConnect())
)
```

A source comment states:

> On Windows we use the official driver name.

However, the current official Databricks ODBC driver installer for Windows (version 2.12.1) registers the driver under the name **`"Databricks ODBC Driver"`**, not `"Databricks"`. This is visible both via `odbc::odbcListDrivers()` and directly in the Windows registry:

```
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\ODBC\ODBCINST.INI\ODBC Drivers
    "Databricks ODBC Driver" = "Installed"

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\ODBC\ODBCINST.INI\Databricks ODBC Driver
    Description = "Databricks ODBC Driver"
    Driver      = "C:\Program Files\Databricks ODBC Driver\lib\DatabricksODBC64.dll"
```

Since neither `"Databricks"` nor `"Simba Spark ODBC Driver"` matches this registered name, auto-detection fails even though the driver is correctly installed:

```r
odbc::odbcListDrivers()
#>                     name    attribute                  value
#> ...
#> 22   Databricks ODBC Driver Description Databricks ODBC Driver
DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::databricks(),
  workspace = "https://<workspace>.azuredatabricks.net",
  httpPath  = "/sql/protocolv1/o/.../..."
)
#> Error in `DBI::dbConnect()`:
#> ! Failed to automatically find the Databricks/Spark ODBC driver.
#> ℹ Set `driver` to known driver name or path.
```

Passing `driver = "Databricks ODBC Driver"` explicitly works fine:

```r
DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::databricks(),
  driver    = "Databricks ODBC Driver",
  workspace = "https://<workspace>.azuredatabricks.net",
  httpPath  = "/sql/protocolv1/o/.../..."
)
#> works
```

**Suggested fix:** add `"Databricks ODBC Driver"` to the `fallbacks` vector in `databricks_default_driver()`:

```r
fallbacks = c("Databricks", "Databricks ODBC Driver", "Simba Spark ODBC Driver")
```

**Environment:**

```
R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24 ucrt)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64
Running under: Windows 11 x64 (build 26200)

odbc 1.7.0
DBI 1.3.0

Databricks ODBC Driver 2.12.1, installed via the official Databricks Windows installer
```

title: `databricks()` silently truncates STRING columns at 1,023 characters
description:
## What happens

`odbc::databricks()` returns STRING columns truncated to 1,023 characters, with no warning, no error and no condition raised. The value you get back is a valid 1,023-character string, so a caller cannot distinguish it from genuinely short data without independently knowing the true length.

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::databricks(), httpPath = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_PATH"))
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT repeat('x', 5000) AS s")$s |> nchar()
#> 1023
```

Passing `DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535` to `dbConnect()` fixes it completely:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::databricks(),
  httpPath = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_PATH"),
  DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535
)
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT repeat('x', 5000) AS s")$s |> nchar()
#> 5000
```

On v1.7.0, pass `65535` rather than a rounder `100000`: see the #934 interaction below.

Nothing about this is specific to Databricks' spatial or nested types. `repeat('x', n)` is enough, and any free-text column, notes field, JSON blob or WKT geometry over 1,023 characters is affected.

## The boundary is exactly 1,023/1,024

| Characters requested | Default | `DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535` |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1,000 | 1,000 |
| 1,023 | 1,023 | 1,023 |
| 1,024 | **1,023** | 1,024 |
| 2,000 | **1,023** | 2,000 |
| 5,000 | **1,023** | 5,000 |
| 20,000 | **1,023** | 20,000 |

## Why the silence is the problem

The truncation itself is a driver default and arguably working as configured. What makes it bite is that nothing tells you it happened.

I tested for that directly rather than inferring it from console output. Wrapping the 5,000-character query in `withCallingHandlers()` and capturing both condition classes:

```r
w <- NULL; m <- NULL
res <- withCallingHandlers(
  DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT repeat('x', 5000) AS s"),
  warning = function(c) { w <<- conditionMessage(c); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") },
  message = function(c) { m <<- conditionMessage(c); invokeRestart("muffleMessage") }
)
w              #> NULL
m              #> NULL
nchar(res$s)   #> 1023
```

No condition of any kind is signalled. The truncation is a clean prefix, not corruption: for the 5,000-character case the returned value is byte-identical to `strrep("x", 1023)`, so the first 1,023 characters are right and the remainder is simply absent.

## This compounds with #934 on the current release

#934 reported that `build_connection_string()` renders large numerics in scientific notation, and
the reporter hit it with `DefaultStringColumnLength` specifically: `100000` became `1e+05`, which the driver silently ignored. That is fixed by #1016, merged after v1.7.0 shipped, so it is not in the current CRAN release.

The two interact badly on 1.7.0. The truncation is silent, and the workaround for it is also silently dropped if you pick a round number:

```r
odbc:::build_connection_string(list(DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535))
#> "DefaultStringColumnLength=65535"    # fine
odbc:::build_connection_string(list(DefaultStringColumnLength = 100000))
#> "DefaultStringColumnLength=1e+05"    # silently ignored by the driver
```

It is not a simple size threshold, which makes it harder to spot. R uses scientific notation only when it is shorter than the fixed form, so round numbers are the ones that break while longer values pass:

| Value passed | Rendered on 1.7.0 |
|---|---|
| `65535` | `65535` |
| `99999` | `99999` |
| `100000` | `1e+05` |
| `123456` | `123456` |
| `200000` | `2e+05` |
| `1000000` | `1e+06` |

On 1.7.0 the working forms are a literal string `"100000"`, an integer `100000L`, or `format(100000, scientific = FALSE)`. Note that `as.character(100000)` does **not** work, because the coercion happens before the string is built and yields `"1e+05"`.

So a user on the current release who hits the truncation, finds `DefaultStringColumnLength`, and reaches for a round number gets a fix that appears to do nothing. Two silent failures in sequence.

## Suggestion

Since `databricks()` exists to supply sensible defaults for this backend, the fix probably belongs there rather than in every caller. Either:

- set a larger `DefaultStringColumnLength` in `databricks()` by default, or
- document in `?databricks` that the driver default caps STRING at 1,023 characters, and name `DefaultStringColumnLength` as the remedy

I have no view on which is right, and the first may well have memory implications you understand better than I do. #856 covers similar ground for `EnableQueryResultDownload`, another Simba parameter with an awkward default, and the discussion there leaned towards documenting rather than overriding a Databricks default. That issue is still open, so I am reading it as related prior discussion rather than a settled precedent. Happy to send a PR for either once you have picked.

If it stays a documentation change, the `?databricks` note is more useful if it names a value that survives #934 on the current release, or points at the string form.

## Environment

```
R 4.5.2 (2025-10-31)
odbc 1.7.0
DBI 1.3.0
driver: RStudio Pro Drivers, Spark ODBC 2.7.7.1016 (libsparkodbc_sb64.so)
DBSQL 2026.20, Azure Databricks serverless SQL warehouse
```

Reproduced on two separate sessions, 2026-08-18 and 2026-08-20, with identical results at every size in the table above.

## What I have not established

The scope here is narrow and I would rather say so than have you assume otherwise:

- one warehouse, one DBSQL version (2026.20), one driver version (2.7.7.1016), so this says nothing about other versions
- serverless SQL warehouse only, with no all-purpose cluster or DBR path tested
- no intermediate `DefaultStringColumnLength` values tried, so I cannot say where the useful floor sits between the default and 65535
- I have not read the driver's own documentation on what its default actually is, so I cannot confirm 1,023 is the documented figure rather than an artefact of this setup

title: override built-in connection arguments case-insensitively
description:
#1026 had originally tackled this:

> User-supplied connection arguments now override built-in defaults case-insensitively. Connection string keys are case-insensitive to drivers, and users following the driver docs will pass DefaultStringColumnLength (PascalCase); previously that would have been emitted alongside our camelCase default as a duplicate key. This also fixes the same latent hazard for existing defaults like thriftTransport.

Some discussion in https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/pull/1026#discussion_r3875633736_. That change seems worth doing, but ought to be considered separately.

title: Add ambient detection for Connect service account credentials to `odbc::snowflake()`
description:
## Summary

`snowflake_auth_args()` detects Posit Connect credentials only through `connectcreds::has_viewer_token()`. There is no equivalent check for
`connectcreds::has_service_account_token()`, so content deployed to Connect with a **service account** OAuth integration cannot use ambient credentials.  `connectcreds` now supports this flow.

The result is that `DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake(), ...)` fails with a message:

```
Failed to detect ambient Snowflake credentials.
i Supply `uid` and `pwd` to authenticate manually.
i Or consider enabling Posit Connect's Snowflake integration for viewer-based
  credentials.
```

A valid integration is enabled and attached to the content item but it is a service account type, not viewer.

## Workaround

Fetch and pass the token manually with `connectcreds`:

```r
token <- connectcreds::connect_service_account_token()
DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::snowflake(),
  authenticator = "oauth",
  token = token$access_token,
  database = "MY_DB",
  schema = "PUBLIC"
)
```

## Session info

```
odbc 1.7.0
connectcreds 0.2.0
snowflakeauth 0.2.2
DBI 1.3.0
```

title: Add support for Posit Connect service account flow with Databricks using `connectcreds`

It would be helpful for those using "Service Account" style credentials to be able to use the same helper function. It looks like `connectcreds` already has the functionality needed:

title: Numeric connection string parameters may be formatted incorrectly in connection string
description:
Hi odbc team,

`odbc:::build_connection_string` creates a connection string out of the parameters passed to `DBI::dbConnect`/`odbc:::odbc_connect`. In the case one of the parameters is a large numeric, it may be converted to scientific format, potentially yielding an incorrect or invalid connection string.

This has happened to me with the [Simba Spark ODBC Driver](https://docs.databricks.com/_extras/documents/Simba-Apache-Spark-ODBC-Connector-Install-and-Configuration-Guide.pdf) `DefaultStringColumnLength` argument/connection attribute. My data contains a field that may store long JSON strings, hence I set `DefaultStringColumnLength` to a large number to err on the safe side
```r
DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc(),
  Driver                    = "Simba Spark ODBC Driver",
  SparkServerType           = 3,
  Host                      = "[MY_HOST]",
  Port                      = 443,
  AuthMech                  = 3,
  UID                       = "token",
  PWD                       = "[MY_TOKEN]",
  ThriftTransport           = 2,
  HTTPPath                  = "[MY_PATH]",
  DefaultStringColumnLength = 100000
)
```
which leads to the following connection string generated by `odbc:::build_connection_string` 
```r
[1] "Driver=Simba Spark ODBC Driver;SparkServerType=3;...;DefaultStringColumnLength=1e+05"
```
The `DefaultStringColumnLength=1e+05` part is silently ignored by the driver.

The workaround I currently use it to set the parameter to a string directly (`DefaultStringColumnLength = "100000"`). However, it may be nicer if these cases are handled in the package directly. This issue could be solved by changing the definition of `odbc:::build_connection_string` to explicitly avoid scientific notation with `format(args, scientific = FALSE)` instead of using `args` directly:
```r
build_connection_string <- function(args = list(), string = NULL) {

  args_string <- paste(names(args), format(args, scientific = FALSE), sep = "=", collapse = ";")

  if (!is.null(string) && !grepl(";$", string) && length(args) > 0) {
    string <- paste0(string, ";")
  }

  paste0(string, args_string)
}
```
which yields
```r
[1] "Driver=Simba Spark ODBC Driver;SparkServerType=3;...;DefaultStringColumnLength=100000"
```

description:
Hi folks, when making multiple `dbConnect(odbc::snowflake())` calls in sequence (during a test suite that builds several database connections) we intermittently get:

~~~
Error: ! ODBC failed with error 00000 from [RStudio][Snowflake].
✖  (16)
•  Unexpected exception: ReauthenticationRequest Signal Exception
• 
ℹ From nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1184.
~~~

We're not sure what is causing the error, and given the characteristics of it I'm unable to provide a reprex. 
We're using the Workbench managed credentials path, where `odbc::snowflake()` reads the token from the `connections.toml` file.

The same call succeeds immediately on manual retry with no session restart, no credential refresh, and no code change. It is never observed when making a single connection in isolation.

We tried adding an automated re-try to the `dbConnect` call, but the error stills comes up even after 2 re-tries with a 5 sec separation window.
We also noticed the error is more frequent in Workbench RStudio than in Workbench Positron (using the same test suite).

**Environment**

  - `odbc` 1.6.4 and 1.7.0 (reproduced on both)

title: Allowing non-local characters on Windows
description:
Since in this package nanodbc was compiled without the flag `NANODBC_USE_UNICODE`, all connections are established in A mode and not in W mode. Systems that are not running with a UTF locale, but for example `German_Germany.1252`, do not support the transmission of special characters outside of this encoding (in the following I will simplify by assuming `Latin-1`).
This affects (even though R now supports it) almost all Windows clients, since the use of `UTF-8` C locales in windows is only supported as beta.

This leads to the situation that queries via `dbGetQuery` containing non-`Latin-1` characters reach the database without the special characters and thus produce incorrect results. And in the opposite direction, queries containing non-`Latin-1` characters cannot be properly received.

I believe this could also be the underlying problem in the  issues #301 and #479

The simplest solution would be to compile nanodbc with the flag `NANODBC_USE_UNICODE`. I have not yet been able to test this, but a first look at the code suggests to me that only minor changes would be necessary. Since nanodbc always uses `UTF-8` as the return encoding for Unicode strings, this also covers `UTF-16LE` as used in the odbc W mode.

If I am mistaken, I would be very grateful for a solution. Here is my situation:

- Server: SQL Server 2022
- Client: Windows 11
- Tested under 4.1.2, 4.4.1 and 4.5.1
- Local: `German_Germany.1252`
- Connection via
```R
DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc(),
  Driver = "ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server",
  Server = server_name,
  Database = db_name,
  Trusted_Connection = "yes",
  encoding = "latin1"
)
```

title: wstring_convert::to_bytes crash when Snowflake ODBC metadata contains non-ASCII characters in view REMARKS
description:
When using odbc in Snowflake, we ran across an issue where we couldn't list connections:

```
> conn <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake())
+ connections::connection_view(conn)
Error:
! wstring_convert::to_bytes
```

After doing some digging we noticed it's specific to `SNOWFLAKE_PUBLIC_DATA_FREE` which contains data with special characters like `é` and `§`. Setting `Sys.setlocale("LC_ALL", "en_US.UTF-8")` does not resolve it.

Steps to reproduce:

The error surfaces when connecting without scoping to a specific database, so that SQLTables enumerates all catalogs:

```
library(DBI)
library(odbc)

conn <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake())
DBI::dbListTables(conn)
# Error: wstring_convert::to_bytes
```



It can be reproduced against any Snowflake account with access to the `SNOWFLAKE_PUBLIC_DATA_FREE`, which contains views with non-ASCII characters in their comments:

# Confirm the offending characters
```
view_info <- DBI::dbGetQuery(conn, "
  SELECT TABLE_NAME, COMMENT 
  FROM SNOWFLAKE_PUBLIC_DATA_FREE.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS
  WHERE COMMENT IS NOT NULL AND COMMENT != ''
")
```

`non_ascii <- view_info[grepl("[^\x01-\x7F]", view_info$COMMENT, perl = TRUE), ]`

# Extract the specific characters
```
chars <- regmatches(non_ascii$COMMENT, gregexpr("[^\x01-\x7F]", non_ascii$COMMENT, perl = TRUE))
sort(unique(unlist(chars)))
# Includes: é and §
```

These characters cannot be converted to ASCII:
```
iconv(paste(sort(unique(unlist(chars))), collapse = ""), from = "UTF-8", to = "ASCII")
[1] NA
```



Traceback

```
1. +-connections::connection_view(conn)
2. \-connections:::dbi_schemas(con)
3.   \-DBI::dbListObjects(con)
4.     \-odbc::dbListTables(conn)
5.       \-odbc:::odbcConnectionTables(...)
6.         \-odbc:::connection_sql_tables(...)
Error: wstring_convert::to_bytes
```

Expected behavior

Non-ASCII characters in ODBC metadata (specifically the REMARKS column returned by SQLTables) should be handled gracefully, either by using std::codecvt_utf8<wchar_t> explicitly in wstring_convert, or by substituting/skipping unconvertible characters.


Root cause

The C++ code in connection_sql_tables uses `std::wstring_convert` with a locale-dependent codecvt facet to convert ODBC wide-string metadata to narrow strings. The ODBC SQLTables call returns the REMARKS column for all views, and when any view comment contains a non-ASCII character (e.g., é, §), the conversion throws `std::range_error`. Setting the R/C locale via Sys.setlocale() does not affect the C++ locale used by std::wstring_convert. The fix would be to use std::codecvt_utf8<wchar_t> explicitly.

Session info

R version 4.5.1
odbc 1.7.0
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
Positron 2026.05.2

title: `odbc::databricks()` fails with new Databricks ODBC driver install path on macOS
description:
`DBI::dbConnect(odbc::databricks(), ...)` fails with the new Databricks ODBC driver (installed from [the official site](https://www.databricks.com/spark/odbc-drivers-download)) on macOS. The new driver installs to `/Library/databricks/databricksodbc/` rather than the legacy Simba Spark path at `/Library/simba/spark/`. This is noted in their own documentation that ships along with the installed driver.
See Documentation Screencap
### Error `Error in file(con, "r") : invalid 'description' argument` ### Root cause `spark_simba_config()` doesn't recognize the new driver path and returns `character(0)` for the config file path: ```r odbc:::spark_simba_config("/Library/databricks/databricksodbc/lib/libdatabricksodbc.dylib" ) #> $path #> character(0) #> #> $url #> [1] "https://www.databricks.com/spark/odbc-drivers-download" ``` `configure_simba()` then tries to open `character(0)` as a file, causing the error. ### Reproduction ```r # odbc 1.6.4.1, macOS 15 (Darwin 25.3.0) # Databricks ODBC driver installed at /Library/databricks/databricksodbc/ DBI::dbConnect( odbc::databricks(), httpPath = "/sql/1.0/warehouses/example", driver = "/Library/databricks/databricksodbc/lib/libdatabricksodbc.dylib" ) #> Error in file(con, "r") : invalid 'description' argument ``` ### Workaround Using odbc::odbc() directly with explicit parameters works: ``` DBI::dbConnect( odbc::odbc(), driver = "/Library/databricks/databricksodbc/lib/libdatabricksodbc.dylib", host = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_HOST"), port = 443, AuthMech = 3, httpPath = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH"), protocol = "https", thriftTransport = 2, ssl = 1, uid = "token", pwd = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_TOKEN") ) ``` ### Environment - odbc version: 1.6.4.1 - macOS (Darwin 25.3.0) - Driver: Databricks ODBC driver at /Library/databricks/databricksodbc/lib/libdatabricksodbc.dylib - Driver config: /Library/databricks/databricksodbc/lib/databricks.databricksodbc.ini

title: Crash while using Snowflake sf_private_key key
description:
Hello!

A few months back I created #923.

Back then it worked flawlessly but when I tried again today I stumbled across a session crash. I'm using the same snippet as back then:

```
con <- dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc(),
  driver = "SnowflakeDSIIDriver",
  server = "XXX",
  uid = "YYY",
  authenticator = "snowflake_jwt",
  attributes = list("sf_private_key" = pk),
)
```
**The R session crashes with a coredump: `corrupted size vs. prev_size`.**

**I found out that if I remove the last `\n` of the private key it works normally. I'm just using `sub("\n$", "", pk)`.**

The difference is exactly 1 character:

```
nchar(pk_raw)
[1] 1704
nchar(pk_fixed)
[1] 1703

pk_raw: ends with -----END PRIVATE KEY-----\n ←
pk_fixed: ends with -----END PRIVATE KEY----- ←
```

However, from what I know the last `\n` in an openssh private key file is perfectly normal. I checked straigth from keys created using `ssh-keygen`:

```
0000640   D       O   P   E   N   S   S   H       P   R   I   V   A   T
0000660   E       K   E   Y   -   -   -   -   -  \n
0000673
```

And the openssh library also reports the key to be vaild before removing the last `\n`.

```
library(openssl)
Linking to: OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024
tryCatch({
+   read_key(pk)
+   message("Key format is valid!")
+ }, error = function(e) {
+   message("Key format invalid: ", e$message)
+ })
Key format is valid!
```

```r
dbWriteTable(con, tbl_name, data.frame(int = 2L, tm = tm_tz2), append = TRUE)

dbWriteTable(con, tbl_name, data.frame(int = 4:6, tm = c(tm_tz1_chr, tm_tz2_chr, tm_utc_chr)), append = TRUE)

rets <- lapply(1:6, function(int) {
  dbGetQuery(con, paste("select int, tm, cast(tm as varchar(max)) as tm_chr from", tbl_name,
```

title: r crash on dbBind
description:

title: sqlserver datetimeoffset is wrong
description:
I have a table column `sessions.scheduledstart` that is stored as a `datetimeoffset`.

```r
x <- dbGetQuery(con, "select scheduledstart, cast(scheduledstart as varchar(36)) as time from sessions where id='6E1B7023-31B7-EF11-A2EB-D094661AB20E'")
x
#        scheduledstart                               time
# 1 2025-11-02 10:00:00 2025-11-02 15:00:00.0000000 -05:00

attr(x$scheduledstart, "tzone")
# [1] "UTC"
```

The `time` above is the untouched-by-`odbc` value, and it shows `15:00:00 -05:00`. By the comment in https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/pull/951#issue-3485002962 and the assumption that `odbc` uses the ISO8601 interpretation for offset, negative means that the time is _West_ of Greenwich. Since the `"tzone"` of the returned value is "UTC", this means that the time should be showing `20:00:00`.

```r
as.POSIXct(sub(":00$", "00", x$time), format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS %z", tz = "UTC")
# [1] "2025-11-02 20:00:00 UTC"
```

title: Feature Request: Support for Azure AD Access Token Authentication (SQL_COPT_SS_ACCESS_TOKEN)
description:
The odbc package currently does not support Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) access token authentication for Microsoft SQL Server connections. This limits the ability to connect to Azure SQL Database using modern authentication methods, particularly when Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) is enforced.

Microsoft SQL Server ODBC drivers support Azure AD access tokens via the SQL_COPT_SS_ACCESS_TOKEN connection attribute (value 1256). The token must be passed as a binary structure before calling SQLDriverConnect():

title: Document `EnableQueryResultDownload` for `databricks()`
description:
Without setting `EnableQueryResultDownload='0'` in the Databricks connection string, queries of > ~40k rows will return no data and a relatively cryptic error message:


> [Simba][Hardy] (35) Error from server: error code: '0' error message: '[Simba][Hardy] (134) File fe48a1be-0a4e-482e-aa09-3ec21215756d: A retriable error occurred while attempting to download a result file from the cloud store but the retry limit had been exceeded. Error Detail: File fe48a1be-0a4e-482e-aa09-3ec21215756d: An error had occurred while attempting to download the result file.The error is: Couldn't resolve host name. Since the connection has been configured to consider all result file download as retriable errors, we will attempt to retry the download.'.


However, all it takes to solve this is adding `EnableQueryResultDownload='0'` to the connection string or DBI() call. Then all rows will be returned.

This isn't found anywhere within Databricks' documentation, and figuring it out involves a fair bit of Stack Overflow sleuthing. It's also very different behavior compared to many other DBI connections, which could lead to extra confusion. I think it would be helpful to include this tip in the documentation for `odbc::databricks()`.

title: `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` returns offset in time despite specifying `timezone =` in `dbConnect()` with Oracle
description:
Using Oracle, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` returns a date-time with an offset in time despite specifying `timezone =` in `dbConnect()`:

```r
library(DBI)

Sys.setenv(TZ = "Europe/Paris")
Sys.time()
# [1] "2023-12-14 18:01:37 CET"

query <- "SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AS DTE FROM DUAL;"

conn <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                  dsn = "xxx",
                  timezone = "Europe/Paris",
                  timezone_out = "Europe/Paris")
dbGetQuery(conn, query)$DTE
# [1] "2023-12-14 17:01:40 CET"
dbDisconnect(conn)
```

[`ORA_SDTZ`](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E18283_01/server.112/e10729/ch4datetime.htm#insertedID9) must be set to get the correct result:

```r
Sys.setenv(ORA_SDTZ = "Europe/Paris")

conn <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                  dsn = "xxx",
                  timezone = "Europe/Paris",
                  timezone_out = "Europe/Paris")
dbGetQuery(conn, query)$DTE
# [1] "2023-12-14 18:01:46 CET"
dbDisconnect(conn)
```

OTOH, specifying `timezone =` in `dbConnect()` is sufficient to get correct date-times using `TIMESTAMP`:

```r
query <- "SELECT TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01 12:00:00' AS DTE FROM DUAL;"

Sys.setenv(ORA_SDTZ = "")
conn <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                  dsn = "xxx",
                  timezone = "Europe/Paris",
                  timezone_out = "Europe/Paris")
dbGetQuery(conn, query)$DTE
# [1] "2020-01-01 12:00:00 CET"
dbDisconnect(conn)
```

title: Issue with CASE block against an Oracle DB
description:
I don't get that.

In R, running such a query against Oracle, via a call to odbc::dbGetQuery(con, query):

    SELECT
        em_id,
        status,
        CASE
            WHEN bl_id IS NOT NULL AND fl_id IS NOT NULL
            THEN CONCAT(bl_id, fl_id)
            ELSE NULL
        END AS location
    FROM em;

will return:

    Error: nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1752: HY000:
    [Oracle][ODBC][Ora]ORA-00933: SQL command not properly ended

On the other hand, almost the same one:

    SELECT
        em_id,
        CASE
            WHEN bl_id IS NOT NULL AND fl_id IS NOT NULL
            THEN CONCAT(bl_id, fl_id)
            ELSE NULL
        END,
        status
    FROM em;

will succeed!?

What makes the first request fail?

- The CASE block just before the FROM, and
- The name given to it (AS location)

Only when both previous conditions are false does the query succeed...

NOTE that both queries are correctly run (via dbGetQuery) against an SQL Server DB... 

And both queries do work without any errors in
- SQL Server Management Studio (for SQL Server) and
- SQL Developer (for Oracle).

Both queries are semantically and syntactically correct. Though, one does not work from an Rscript to Oracle...

What can I do to make those queries run without errors on both DB from the R script?

description:
Hi
error handling for the error raised by `odbc` is not very friendly for processing:
```r
conn <- DBI::dbConnect(
```

```r
conditionMessage(res)

```
I would expect something like
```r
#[1] "Invalid object name 'nonsense_tbl'."
```
Or at most

I am on odbc 1.5.0

title: `varchar()` measures characters instead of bytes, causing truncation with multibyte UTF-8 strings (SQL Server)
description:
I believe there’s a bug in the `varchar()` helper when used with SQL Server.

https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/c8a2e2622ddd9c3b87a66022e807e9fcbd31edeb/R/aaa-odbc-data-type.R#L119-L128

The SQL Server documentation for [`VARCHAR(n)`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/char-and-varchar-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver17#varchar---n--max--) defines `n` as the **number of bytes**, not characters.
Currently, `varchar()` determines `n` using `nchar(type = "chars")`, which underestimates the required width for multibyte UTF-8 strings. This can cause string truncation when inserting data longer than 255 bytes.

#### Reprex
``` r
string <- paste0("\xe2\x80\x99", paste(rep("a", 255), collapse = ""))
nchar(string)
#> [1] 256
nchar(string, type = "bytes")
#> [1] 258
odbc:::varchar(string) # not 258
#> [1] "varchar(256)"
```

<sup>Created on 2025-10-29 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

#### Expected

`varchar()` should use the **byte length** of the input (`nchar(x, type = "bytes")`) rather than character count.
That aligns with SQL Server’s definition and avoids truncation with UTF-8 input. 
Using byte length instead of character count should not adversely affect other database backends.

#### Proposed change

I think that this would be the cleanest fix, given `nchar()` supports returning the byte count. 

```r
# before
max_length <- max(c(255, nchar(as.character(x))), na.rm = TRUE)

# after
max_length <- max(c(255, nchar(as.character(x), type = "bytes")), na.rm = TRUE)
```

I plan to open a PR with this proposed change.

title: Dates with integer representation cannot be copied to SQL Server
description:
In R 4.5, `seq.Date()` was changed to no longer coerce the internal representation to floating point and instead keeps the dates as integer representation (https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/old/4.5.0/NEWS.R-4.5.0.html)

Since I use `seq.Date()` in my own work over at [ssi-dk/diseasystore](https://github.com/ssi-dk/diseasystore), I started seeing failures in our test workflow that uses SQL Server with errors like:

```
Error in `db_copy_to(dest$con, name, df, overwrite = overwrite, types = types, 
    temporary = temporary, unique_indexes = unique_indexes, indexes = indexes, 
    analyze = analyze, in_transaction = in_transaction, ...)`: Can't copy data to table "#ds_all_dates_tkhMQuqMpA".
Caused by error in `dplyr::db_write_table()`:
! Can't write table table "#ds_all_dates_tkhMQuqMpA".
Caused by error:
! nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:2077: 00000
[Microsoft][ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server]Restricted data type attribute violation
```

After some digging, I tracked the issue back to the internal representation of dates since R 4.5 and I could fix the issue in my own code base my casting to numeric
`as.Date(as.numeric(..))`

Since I assume I am not the only person that will encounter this issue, I have been tinkering with a fix here to help others.

I have a proposed solution in PR #953 that converts Integer Dates to numeric Dates in `sqlData()`

Let me know if you think this is the right place to tackle this problem.

title: SQL Server, "Invalid Descriptor Index" error nanodbc.cpp when varchar(max) column is not the last field
description:
When querying an SQL Server database table which contains `varchar(max)` columns, we get the infamous "Invalid Descriptor Index" error. However, when we move the varchar(max) columns to be the last column in the SQL query, then there is no error and the query result is just fine 🤔

Here's the code to reproduce it:
```
-- create test table in MS-SQL Server
CREATE TABLE ODBC_R_TEST (
	REC_ID integer,
	SUBJECTID integer,
	PARTICIPANTCODE varchar(200),
	MEASUREMENT integer,

);

```
And then in R-studio query the table like so:
```

DBI::dbGetQuery(conn = sqlConn, statement = "SELECT REC_ID, SUBJECTID, PARTICIPANTCODE, MEASUREMENT, ENCOUNTERIDX, VISITDATE, DOB from [LAB123_P01].[dbo].[ODBC_R_TEST]")
```

title: DATETIMEOFFSET converted with wrong sign on offset (times shifted opposite direction)
description: When reading a SQL Server DATETIMEOFFSET column, the package applies the time zone offset in the wrong direction, causing values to be shifted incorrectly (e.g. 2025-05-10 19:00:00 -04:00 becomes 2025-05-10 15:00:00 UTC instead of 23:00 UTC).

title: Misleading documentation of `encoding` prameter
description:
The parameter `encoding` of the function `dbConnect()` is currently described as:

> The text encoding used on the Database. If the database is not using UTF-8 you will need to set the encoding to get accurate re-encoding. 
> See `iconvlist()` for a complete list of available encodings on your system. Note strings are always returned `UTF-8` encoded.

However, the encoding is actually the one used by the odbc driver (via nanodbc) for communication, and is therefore independent of the database. More precisely, since in this package nanodbc was compiled without the flag `NANODBC_USE_UNICODE`, all connections are established in A mode and not in W mode. Thus, the encoding is almost entirely dependent on the client OS.
I would therefore suggest changing the documentation to:

> The text encoding used by the odbc driver. If it is not using `UTF-8` you will need to set the encoding to get accurate re-encoding. 
> The chosen encoding depends on the system locale. See `iconvlist()` for a complete list of available encodings on your system. 
> Note strings are always returned `UTF-8` encoded.

In addition, I would suggest giving the parameter encoding a default of the form
```R
if(.Platform$OS.type == 'windows') 'Latin-1' else 'UTF-8'.
```

title: Snowflake key-pair authentication and key file
description:
I'm using the Snowflake ODBC Driver for Linux with the `SNOWFLAKE_JWT` authenticator.

This authenticator has a parameter called [PRIV_KEY_FILE](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/odbc/odbc-parameters#using-key-pair-authentication), which I use to point to the file containing the private key, inside my `dbConnect()` calls.

From what I understand its not possible to pass key pair itself directly to `dbConnect()` , just the file name containing the key.

Since I'm pulling the key pair from a vault and prefer not to write the key to a file, I tried using the attribute called [SQL_SF_CONN_ATTR_PRIV_KEY ](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/odbc/odbc-api#label-odbc-api-sqlsetconnectattr-specific-behavior).

I see it's not currently supported after checking the attributes listed [here](https://odbc.r-dbi.org/reference/ConnectionAttributes.html).

title: ODBC 1.6.1 incorrectly overwrites a line within simba.sparkodbc.ini with 'libodbcinst.a'
description:
Upgrading ODBC to 1.6.1 ("odbc will now automatically find statically built installations of unixodbc") causes the error listed here (more detail below), under 'Troubleshooting: Apple macOS users':
[https://solutions.posit.co/connections/db/databases/databricks/](url)

Following the instructions I edited the following file:
`/Library/simba/spark/lib/simba.sparkodbc.ini`

to include this line:
`ODBCInstLib=/opt/homebrew/Cellar/unixodbc/2.3.12/lib/libodbcinst.dylib`

Upon trying my connection:
```
con_db <- dbConnect(
  databricks(),
  httpPath = "/sql/1.0/warehouses/12345678910"
)
```

ODBC 1.6.1 overwrites that line to the following:
`ODBCInstLib=/opt/homebrew/Cellar/unixodbc/2.3.12/lib/libodbcinst.a`

Giving the error:
```
Error in `dbConnect()`:
! ODBC failed with error 00000 from [Simba][ODBC][Simba][Support].
✖  (11560) Unable to locate SQLGetPrivateProfileString function: (50483) Could not load shared library, all attempted paths ("",
  "/opt/homebrew/Cellar/unixodbc/2.3.12/lib/libodbcinst.a") failed
ℹ From nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1150.

```
Uninstalling 1.6.1, re-installing 1.6.0, and following the instructions fixes the problem and the connection can again be made.

title: Support for custom env var when passing user token in `DBI::dbConnect(odbc::databricks())`
description:
Connecting to a serverless SQL warehouse from a user access token with `odbc::databricks()` requires setting the Databricks token to a global environment variable named `DATABRICKS_TOKEN`. If a user has their PAT assigned to the global env var `DATABRICKS_TOKEN`:
```r
# This works
conn_1 <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::databricks(),
  workspace = "https://some-corp.cloud.databricks.com",
  httpPath = "sql/1.0/warehouse/e123456789101112"
)

# This also works
conn_2 <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::databricks(),
  workspace = "https://some-corp.cloud.databricks.com",
  token = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_TOKEN"),
  httpPath = "sql/1.0/warehouse/e123456789101112"
)
```

However, the code below fails even if `DATABRICKS_TOKEN_LAB` is set in the `.Renviron` with the user's correct PAT:
```r
# This fails because token is not specifically calling an env var named DATABRICKS_TOKEN
conn_3 <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::databricks(),
  workspace = "https://some-corp.cloud.databricks.com",
  token = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_TOKEN_LAB"), 
  httpPath = "sql/1.0/warehouse/e123456789101112"
)
```

I work with five (💀) Databricks instances at work so being able to connect to the different endpoints (all w/ different PATs) using different env var names would be very helpful. Thanks!

title: DB2 XML columns  (SQL type -370) are only captured in the default block of nanodbc::auto_bind
description: The IBM Db2 driver sends the code -370 for XML column types.  This type code is only captured by the default block of the switch statement in nanodbc::auto_bind. The result is that XML columns get truncated. This issue is related to https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/issues/907

title: SQL_BLOB (-98) column type code falsely classified as string_t in odbc_result::column_types(nanodbc::result const& r)
description:
Th IBM Db2 driver sends the code -98 for BLOB column types. This should be captured by the BINARY block of the switch statement in `odbc_result::column_types(nanodbc::result const& r)`, but unfortunately it falls through it and ends up captured by the default block: 

```
    case SQL_BINARY:
    case SQL_VARBINARY:
    case SQL_LONGVARBINARY:
      types.push_back(raw_t);
      break;
    default:
      types.push_back(string_t);
      signal_unknown_field_type(type, r.column_name(i));
      break; 
````

The following patch solves the issue, but I don't want to submit it as a pull request because it also involves modifying nanodbc.

```
diff --git a/src/nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp b/src/nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp
index 846f038b..1e63bd40 100644
--- a/src/nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp
+++ b/src/nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp
@@ -93,6 +93,10 @@
 #ifndef SQL_SS_UDT
 #define SQL_SS_UDT (-151) // from sqlncli.h
 #endif
+// IBM Db2 specific SQL type for BLOB
+#ifndef SQL_BLOB
+#define SQL_BLOB (-98)
+#endif
 
 // Default to ODBC version defined by NANODBC_ODBC_VERSION if provided.
 #ifndef NANODBC_ODBC_VERSION
@@ -2977,6 +2981,7 @@ private:
             case SQL_VARBINARY:
             case SQL_LONGVARBINARY:
             case SQL_SS_UDT: // MSDN: Essentially, UDT is a varbinary type with additional metadata.
+           case SQL_BLOB:
                 col.ctype_ = SQL_C_BINARY;
                 col.blob_ = true;
                 col.clen_ = 0;
diff --git a/src/odbc_result.cpp b/src/odbc_result.cpp
index 14a8d2b5..7ee34a67 100644
--- a/src/odbc_result.cpp
+++ b/src/odbc_result.cpp
@@ -8,6 +8,10 @@
 #ifndef SQL_SS_TIME2
 #define SQL_SS_TIME2 (-154)
 #endif
+// IBM Db2 specific SQL type for BLOB
+#ifndef SQL_BLOB
+#define SQL_BLOB (-98)
+#endif
 namespace odbc {
 
 using odbc::utils::run_interruptible;
@@ -715,6 +719,7 @@ std::vector<r_type> odbc_result::column_types(nanodbc::result const& r) {
     case SQL_BINARY:
     case SQL_VARBINARY:
     case SQL_LONGVARBINARY:
+    case SQL_BLOB:
       types.push_back(raw_t);
       break;
     default:
```

The following R code can be used to generate a sample table with a 10MB BLOB column:

```
dbExecute(conn, "CREATE TABLE BLOB_TEST (ID INT, DATA BLOB(10485760))")

# Generate 10 MB of binary data (0xAA repeated)
raw_data <- as.raw(rep(0xAA, 10 * 1024 * 1024))

# Insert the data using parameterized query
dbExecute(conn, "INSERT INTO BLOB_TEST (ID, DATA) VALUES (?, ?)", 
          params = list(1L, list(raw_data)))
```

title: SQL compilation error causes R session to hang - [Snowflake] driver
description:
R session hangs when attempting to send a query to Snowflake. It seems that the Snowflake driver errors out but the DBI package does not know how to recover gracefully from that error, so it hangs for ~ 5 - 10 minutes.

This has been reproduced on multiple environments with different versions of Snowflake driver:

title: dbGetQuery() Returns Incorrect NULL Values When Using R ODBC Package on Linux
description:
**Overview:**
When connecting to a DB2 database using the R ODBC package on Linux, null values in a specific column are returned as unreadable characters instead of being correctly identified as NULL.


**Problem Description:**

- A specific column in the database contains null values.
- When querying the table using the R odbc package on Linux, null values are returned as unreadable characters (e.g., @OǋU) instead of NA.


 The same query works correctly with:
- The Python pyodbc package on Linux.
- Both R odbc and Python pyodbc on Windows.



**Reproducible Example:**

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(odbc)

Sys.setenv(CODEPAGE = "819") 
Sys.setenv(DB2CODEPAGE = "819")

connection <- odbc::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
 .connection_string = paste0('DRIVER=', "{IBM DB2 ODBC DRIVER}",
    ';UID=', Sys.getenv("USER"),
    ';PWD=', Sys.getenv("PASSWORD"),
    ';HOSTNAME=', "placeholder_hostname",
    ';DATABASE=', "placeholder_db",
    ';PORT=', "45000",
    ';COMMITONEOF=0;',
    ';NULLS=YES;'),
 encoding = "latin1")

df_test <- odbc::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT column_name FROM table_name WHERE column_name IS NULL FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY")

df_test %>% head()
```

**Expected Behaviour:**

Null values in the column should be represented as NA in the resulting R data frame.

**Observed Behavior:**

Null values are returned as unreadable characters, as shown below:

```r
 column_name
1          @OǋU
2          @OǋU
3          @OǋU
...
```

**Version info:**

- R version: 4.3.2
- R ODBC version: 1.5.0
- ODBC driver: IBM Data Server Driver for ODBC and CLI (64-bit) 11.5.9

title: dbExistsTable() throws error for DB2 temporary tables in version 1.6.0
description:
```
dbExistsTable(conn, Id(schema = "SESSION", table = "MY_TEMP"))
```
throws

```
Error in `$<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, table_remarks, value = NA_character_) : 
  replacement has 1 row, data has 0
Calls: print ... tryCatchList -> tryCatchOne -> doTryCatch -> $<- -> $<-.data.frame`
```

in version 1.6.0 when applied to DB2 global temporary tables (SESSION.* tables). 

In version 1.5.0 dbExistsTable returns FALSE in the same scenario. 

Please refer to https://github.com/nattomi/odbc-dbexiststable-issue for a reproducible example.

Whether dbExistsTable should theoretically return FALSE or TRUE is not quite clear, because temporary tables are also not visible in the system catalog (syscat,tables). However, it should definitely not throw.

title: ```dplyr::copy_to``` fails with POSIXct data on updated SQL Server 2022
description:
On 2025-03-13 a new release of (MS) SQL Server 2022 ( Version: 16.00.4185) was released. The Github Actions for our SCDB package started failing a test. The command that fails is: ```dplyr::copy_to(conn, data_random) ```. I do not have access to this version of the SQL server locally so I have only been able to test using the Github Action - not efficient. The error I get is "[Microsoft][ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server]Invalid SQL data type" - so it is somehow related to ODBC. By testing different datatypes in ```data_random``` I learned that it works fine except if the data include datetime with type POSIXct.

I have tried to peal of some layers and here is a small example:
```
conn <- <your connection to SQL Server 2022 Version: 16.00.4185 >
# Making a minimal test
    data_ok <- data.frame(
      "Date"      = Sys.Date(),
      "character" = "test",
      "integer"   = 1L,
      "numeric"   = 1,
      "logical"   = TRUE
    )

    data_datetime <- data_ok
    data_datetime$datetime <- Sys.time()

    print(conn)
    # Wanted to do
    # my_copy <- dplyr::copy_to(conn, data_datetime)

    DBI::dbWriteTable(conn, "#testthis", value = data_datetime, temporary = TRUE)
    print("testthis done")

    # dplyr::copy_to effectively calls SQL(as_table_path(<string>))
    # First without a datatime column
    DBI::dbWriteTable(conn, DBI::SQL(dbplyr::as_table_path("#testthis2A", conn)), value = data_ok, temporary = TRUE)
    print("testthis2A done")

    # Then with a datatime column
    DBI::dbWriteTable(conn, DBI::SQL("#testthis2B"), value = data_datetime, temporary = TRUE)
    print("testthis2B done")
    # We never get here
```
The only difference between testthis1 and 2B is that the name of the table is wrapped through SQL for 2B. That means that two different versions af dbWriteTable are used due the differences in signatures.
The backtrace information from testthis2B is:

```
[Microsoft][ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server]Invalid SQL data type 
Backtrace:
    ▆
 1. ├─DBI::dbWriteTable(...) at test-getTableSignature.R:314:5
 2. └─DBI::dbWriteTable(...)
 3.   └─odbc (local) .local(conn, name, value, ...)
 4.     ├─DBI::dbAppendTable(...)
 5.     └─odbc::dbAppendTable(...)

 7.         ├─base::tryCatch(...)
 8.         │ └─base (local) tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
 9.         └─odbc:::result_insert_dataframe(rs@ptr, values, batch_rows)
```

I can see that dbWriteTable first calls dbCreateTable before calling dbAppendTable but this is where the complexity in following the S4 signatures and their subtle differences in methods with Github Actions as the only tool to debug made me write this issue - hoping that others can take take it the last steps.

I found the version of the SQL Server here (https://sqlserverbuilds.blogspot.com/2021/07/sql-server-2022-versions.html)

title: Oracle copy_to errors with index
description:
## Issue
I'm running copy_to with odbc connecting to an Oracle database. The command:
```
copy_to(conn,mtcars, indexes = list('mpg'))
```
I ran into an error:
```
Caused by error in `run()`:
! ODBC failed with error 00000 from [Oracle][ODBC][Ora].
✖ ORA-14452: attempt to create, alter or drop an index on temporary table already in use
• Help: https://docs.oracle.com/error-help/db/ora-14452/
```

## Cause
copy_to with index got translated to steps:
1. Create Global Temporary Table
2. Insert data
3. Add index

The temporary oracle table is created with `ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS` https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/bf7cd404b5417b925dbec1026ac559d1ee09d88d/R/driver-oracle.R#L30-L32
And Oracle will lock the metadata for temp table after data is inserted, which forbids further add index command. I can reproduce the error with below sql script:
```
CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE TMP1 (id int) ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS;
INSERT INTO TMP1 VALUES (1);
CREATE INDEX IDX ON TMP1 (id);
```

## Proposed fix
Add Oracle copy_to logic to first add index, then insert data

description:

Trying to automatize the upload of excels files to databricks I encountered an error with `dbWriteTable()`. I'm using a code very much like this one

title: [Oracle] Error when writing/appending more than 1024 rows to table
description:
Hi Team,

One of our customers surfaced this issue using our Oracle odbc driver and the `odbc` and `DBI` packages. I spent some time trying to successfully reproduce. It looks like an issue with the latest version of `odbc` as `1.4.2` seems to work okay.

Issue: https://rstudioide.zendesk.com/agent/tickets/114557

With the following latest stable versions:
```
> packageVersion("odbc")
[1] ‘1.5.0’
> packageVersion("DBI")
[1] ‘1.2.3’
```

```
> odbc::dbGetInfo(con)
...
[1] "Oracle"
$db.version
[1] "12.02.0010"
$odbc.version
[1] "03.52"
$driver.version
[1] "2.0.7.1009"
$odbcdriver.version
[1] "03.80"
...
```

The customer provided reproducible code, which is available in the Zendesk ticket.
Here's the gist of it from my testing:

#### Non-working code
```
con <- dbConnect(drv = odbc::odbc(), dsn = "oracle")

DBI::dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE TEST_TABELL (
    PERIODE_ID      VARCHAR2(6),
    VERDI           NUMBER,
    TEST_ID         VARCHAR2(100),
    SYS_JOBB_ID     VARCHAR2(100),
    TEST_VARIANT    VARCHAR2(10),
    PAKKEVERSJON    VARCHAR2(20),
    SYS_LASTET_DATO DATE
  )"
)

TEST_TABELL <- tibble::tibble(
  PERIODE_ID      = seq(1, 1025) |> stringr::str_pad(6, pad = "0"),
  VERDI           = seq(1, 1025),
  test_id         = "test",
  sys_jobb_id     = "test_jobb",
  test_variant    = "1",
  pakkeversjon    = "1.0.0",
  sys_lastet_dato = lubridate::today()
) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(stringr::str_to_upper)

  DBI::dbAppendTable(
  con,
  name = "TEST_TABELL",
  value = TEST_TABELL
  )
```

Output from running the last `DBI::dbAppendTable` command yields the following error:
```
>   DBI::dbAppendTable(
+   con,
+   name = "TEST_TABELL",
+   value = TEST_TABELL
+   )
Error: nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1783: 00000
[RStudio][OracleOCI] (3000) Oracle Caller Interface: ORA-01861: literal does not match format string
```

No rows in table:
```
> row_count <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM TEST_TABELL")[[1]]
> row_count
[1] 0
```
#### Working code
I just changed the following rows from `1025` to `1024` from the code example above.
```
TEST_TABELL <- tibble::tibble(
  PERIODE_ID      = seq(1, 1024) |> stringr::str_pad(6, pad = "0"),
  VERDI           = seq(1, 1024),
  ...
```

Code produces no output and I can see the rows added to table:
```
> row_count <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM TEST_TABELL")[[1]]
> row_count
[1] 1024
```

---
#### Working older `odbc` verision

If I use an older `odbc` package with the latest `DBI` package, the original working code is successful:

```
> packageVersion("odbc")
[1] ‘1.4.2’
> packageVersion("DBI")
[1] ‘1.2.3’
```

Using `1025` rows to append to table:
```
TEST_TABELL <- tibble::tibble(
  PERIODE_ID      = seq(1, 1025) |> stringr::str_pad(6, pad = "0"),
  VERDI           = seq(1, 1025),
  ...
```

title: odbc locating SQL Server drivers installed via homebrew on macOS running on Apple Silicon
description:
odbc automatically locates db drivers in most cases, but it fails to automatically locate SQL Server drivers [installed with homebrew](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/connect/odbc/linux-mac/install-microsoft-odbc-driver-sql-server-macos?view=sql-server-ver16#microsoft-odbc-18) on macOS running on Apple Silicon. Examples [[1]](https://stackoverflow.com/q/69759250/5783745), [[2]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74685612/cant-open-lib-odbc-driver-18-for-sql-server-in-r-on-macos-cpu-m2).

A way around this is to set `ODBCSYSINI` in `.Renviron`:

```none
ODBCSYSINI=/opt/homebrew/etc
``` 

Without the environment variable set, odbc doesn't locate installed drivers:

```r
odbc::odbcListDrivers()
# [1] name      attribute value    
# <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

title: Determine DATETIME2 precision based on parameter description
description:
Related to: https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/issues/790 https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/issues/208 https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/issues/130

When writing to a datetime/datetime2 target, we use a fixed precision of three decimals to avoid needing to know the user-configurable precision of the datetime2 field.

However, when writing, we attempt to discover the target table column descriptions and pass these down to `nanodbc` via `statement::describe_parameters`.   We do this to avoid (nanodbc) needing to call `SQLDescribeParams` for each of the individual columns/parameters when binding the data buffers.

If we already have the column descriptions, we could have `nanodbc::statement` expose these - see for example `nanodbc::statement::parameter_size(int)` that already does something similar.  Then we can use this API endpoint in `odbc_result` to maybe deduce the parameter precision.

title: `locate_install_unixodbc()` does not work on a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 install
description:
On a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 box @tnederlof and I see the following error when trying to use `dbConnect()`:

```
Unable to locate the unixODBC driver manager
```

On the CRAN release we see no such error, and the driver manager most certainly *is* installed.

We tracked this down to `locate_install_unixodbc()` returning no results, and as of #825 we verify that in `dbConnect()`. I believe this is because it assumes `pkg-config` is available, which it is not on a fresh Ubuntu machine: https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/4ecd5099276e90e2840ff0100bdbed9edcf6f4e2/R/utils.R#L332-L335

There is also a list of "common" paths: https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/4ecd5099276e90e2840ff0100bdbed9edcf6f4e2/R/utils.R#L341-L348

But this does not include the path `libodbcinst.so` is actually installed to, which is under `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`.

I believe this can be fixed by adding that path to the common list; it should fix issues on many Debian-derived distros. We could also advise that folks install `pkg-confg`, but that seems wrong to me.

I think we should try to build these out over time.

title: SQL Server requires `varchar(max)` and `varbinary(max)` columns to be at the end of `SELECT` statements.
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
SQL Server requires `varchar(max)` and `varbinary(max)` columns to be at the end of `SELECT` statements. If they are before the end a `[Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server]Invalid Descriptor Index` error is returned. This is apparently a [known workaround](http://stackoverflow.com/a/17566753/2055486) for this problem.

### Database
SQL Server 2013 (13.00.1601)

### Reproducible Example
``` r
library(DBI);library(odbc)
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), "test")

# Reorder columns and put the species column first
it <- iris[1:10, c(5, 1, 2)]
dbWriteTable(con, "it", it)
#> [1] TRUE

# SELECT using normal order with varchar(max) first
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * from it")
#> Warning in value[[3L]](cond): nanodbc.cpp:2755: 07009: [Microsoft][ODBC
#> Driver 13 for SQL Server]Invalid Descriptor Index
#> Warning: Pending rows
#> NULL

# However SELECT using varchar(max) at the end work fine
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT \"Sepal.Length\", \"Sepal.Width\", Species from it")
#>    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Species
#> 1           5.1         3.5  setosa
#> 2           4.9         3.0  setosa
#> 3           4.7         3.2  setosa
#> 4           4.6         3.1  setosa
#> 5           5.0         3.6  setosa
#> 6           5.4         3.9  setosa
#> 7           4.6         3.4  setosa
#> 8           5.0         3.4  setosa
#> 9           4.4         2.9  setosa
#> 10          4.9         3.1  setosa
```

title: Encoding/Collation problems with 1.5.0 SQL server
description:
We have been expriencing encoding problems with odbc 1.5.0 on SQL server. This works fine on odbc 1.4.2

All our databases unfortunately uses the varchar collation "Danish_Norwegian_CI_AS" - with odbc 1.4.2 however we were able to create a connection so that we could correctly read and write to the database. With odbc 1.5.0 the column names are no longer formatted correctly.

Is this a bug or can we change the connection settings so that it works correctly?

``` r
library('magrittr')
conn <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc()
  , Driver = "ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server"
  , Server = "server"
  , Database = 'database'
  , Trusted_Connection = "Yes"
  , encoding = 'latin1'
  , AutoTranslate = 'no'
)

test_table <- DBI::Id(schema = 'test', table = 'test_table')
df <- tibble::tibble(
  var_char_col = c('kanin', 'ræven', 'ålens', 'ørred'),
  bøvs = 1
)


DBI::dbWriteTable(
  conn
  , name = test_table
  , df
  , field.types = c('var_char_col' = 'varchar(5)')
  , overwrite = TRUE
)

db_data <- DBI::dbReadTable(conn, test_table) %>%
  tibble::as_tibble()

db_data
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   var_char_col bÃ.vs
#>   <chr>        <dbl>
#> 1 kanin            1
#> 2 ræven            1
#> 3 ålens            1
#> 4 ørred            1
```

Expected value:
``` r
db_data
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   var_char_col  bøvs
#>   <chr>        <dbl>
#> 1 kanin            1
#> 2 ræven            1
#> 3 ålens            1
#> 4 ørred            1
```

If we remove the encoding parameter - we get correct colum names, however the character vector no longer fit within the varchar(5) datatype even though we only have 5 characters:

``` r
library('magrittr')
conn <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc()
  , Driver = "ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server"
  , Server = "server"
  , Database = 'database'
  , Trusted_Connection = "Yes"
  # , encoding = 'latin1'
  , AutoTranslate = 'no'
)

test_table <- DBI::Id(schema = 'test', table = 'test_table')
df <- tibble::tibble(
  var_char_col = c('kanin', 'ræven', 'ålens', 'ørred'),
  bøvs = 1
)


DBI::dbWriteTable(
  conn
  , name = test_table
  , df
  , field.types = c('var_char_col' = 'varchar(5)')
  , overwrite = TRUE
)
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1783: 00000
#> [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server]String data, right truncation

db_data <- DBI::dbReadTable(conn, test_table) %>%
  tibble::as_tibble()

db_data
#> # A tibble: 0 × 2
#> # ℹ 2 variables: var_char_col <chr>, bøvs <dbl>
```

title: bit64 integer64 is broken and should not be used
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
bit64 is fundamentally broken. Examples:
```r
317.15 / bit64::as.integer64(25) == 317.15 / 25L
# FALSE # 12.68 vs 12.686

# From https://github.com/truecluster/bit64/issues/12 :
3.5 * bit64::as.integer64(6) == bit64::as.integer64(6) * 3.5
# FALSE # 18 vs 21
```

Thus odbc should never convert to bit64 integer64. Unfortunately newer databases (e.g. Redshift / Athena) return COUNT() and SUM(some_int) as bigint and the default option for dbGetQuery is bigint = "integer64".

Unfortunately it also looks like bit64 has been abandoned. The underlying issues might not be a big deal as there are even pull requests for the above mentioned #12 here: https://github.com/truecluster/bit64/pull/13. But no change since 2 1/2 years.

### Database
Any database that has bigint. For example Redshift or Athena.

### Reproducible Example

```r
library(odbc)
library(DBI)
library(tidyverse)

rs_con <- odbc::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), "Redshift")
test <- odbc::dbGetQuery(rs_con, "SELECT CAST(25 as BIGINT) as int64")

test %>% 
  mutate(
    v1 = 317.15 / int64
    , v2 = 317.15 / as.numeric(int64)
    , v1 == v2 # FALSE
  )

test <- odbc::dbGetQuery(rs_con, "SELECT CAST(25 as BIGINT) as int64")
test %>% 
  mutate(
    v1 = 3.5 * int64
    , v2 = int64 * 3.5
    , v1 == v2 # FALSE
  )

```

title: `setMethod("sqlData", "OdbcConnection")` should use `inherits`
description: Rather than `is()` and `is.object()`.

title: dbWriteTable uses `BIT` datatype instead of `BOOL`
description:
When the `dbms.name` is `NetezzaSQL` then `dbWriteTable` should write a logical TRUE/FALSE data column as type `BOOL` as per this list of supported data types: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/netezza?topic=vc-data-types-aliases

Instead, it seems to be trying to use the `BIT` datatype, which is not supported by Netezza.

Example:
```r
a = data.frame(Test = runif(100) > 0.5)
dbWriteTable(n_con, "TEST_DELETE", a)
```
results in
```r
Error in `dbWriteTable()`:
! ODBC failed with error HY000 from .
✖ ERROR: transformColumnType: error reading type 'BIT'
• <SQL> 'CREATE TABLE "TEST_DELETE" (
•  "Test" BIT
• )
• '
```

title: chore: clean up `check_*` in dbi-driver
description:
There are a number of arguments ( `encoding`, `timezone`, `timeout`, etc ) for which `allow_null` is set to `TRUE` on one hand, and on the other we simply pass them through the C/++ layer ( where they are strongly typed ).

* Verify that in fact they are not allowed to be `NULL` ( expect `Rcpp` to complain ).
* Update the arguments to the `check_*` methods; probably better to throw a nicely formatted error.

title: Allow the user to override parameter metadata
description:
Currently, the implementation for SQL server does not allow for unicode support when writing tables, quoting literals, or using parameters.

This leads to tables being created without unicode support or special unicode characters, and queries being created with literals without special unicode characters, leading to a comparison with a non-ascii unicode character returning the wrong results.

There have been some issues, like https://github.com/r-dbi/DBI/issues/215, where it's suggested to encode strings as bytes, but that results in fragile code that relies on specific SQL server settings and locales, and only solves specific issues like writing tables. I'd like to write code that "just works" if at all possible.

``` r
library(DBI)
#> Warning: package 'DBI' was built under R version 4.1.3
library(odbc)
conn <- dbConnect(odbc(), driver = "ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server", server = "localhost", database = "example", trusted_connection = "yes", encoding = "utf-8")
unicode_string <- "\u2915"
odbc::dbQuoteString(conn, unicode_string) # Expected: <SQL> N'⤕'
#> <SQL> '<U+2915>'
odbc::odbcDataType(conn, unicode_string) # Expected: nvarchar(255)
#> [1] "varchar(255)"
dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT ?", params = list(unicode_string)) # Expected: 1  '⤕'
#>    
#> 1 ?

# Note that the connection does support it and properly returns the expected character
dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT N'\u2915'")
#>           
#> 1 <U+2915>
```
