description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

Using `dbExecute()` (and possibly other functions) on a DB2 connection that was configured with `autocommit = 0` do not work. If you call `dbExecute()`, close the connection and reconnect to the database, the next SQL Statement will cause R to become nonresponsive. 

Everything works just fine with `dbBegin() .... dbCommit()`. I am not sure what the expected behaviour is, but I assume `dbExecute()` is supposed to take care of such things? There also seems no way to manually commit when you use `dbExecute()`. It's hard for me to give more details, since I am not the person responsible for configuring our DB2 servers.

### Example
Reproducible, but requires a DB2 server configured in the way described above

```r
library(odbc)
library(DBI)

# everything below works
con <- # establish db2 connection
DBI::dbExecute(con, "create table TMP.TEST (tcol char(3))")
print(DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "select * from TMP.TEST"))
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)


# This causes R to become nonresponsive 
con <-  # establish db2 connection again
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "select * from TMP.TEST")
```

title: Switch to change default Timezone behaviour
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
Currently, even though the timezone parameter is set when using dbconnect time still come back from dB queries as UTC. Although the dates returned are technically correct it is less than useful for data to show in the view or console output as 2018-04-22 14:00 UTC when the real value should be 2018-04-23 AEST, which is the value returned by RODBC queries.
This is especially painful when looking at large data frames containing multiple date columns as in View() the timezone isn’t visible. Although I believe you can override this by setting datecolumn <- c(datecolumn) it is inefficient for large datasets (24+m rows), and the conversion is likely performed twice - once to UTC and once back to the desired timezone.

### Possible solution
A parameter on the dbconnect and/or the query functions in odbc to override the default “convert to UTC” behaviour to instead utilise the timezone that has been provided on the connection. This would default to the current behaviour but at least allow users to obtain RODBC equivalent behaviour where desired.

title: Show first and last 4000 characters of error message if too long
description:
Error messages can't be arbitrarily long in R:

``` r
tryCatch(
  stop(paste(sample(letters, 100000, replace = TRUE))),
  error = function(e) nchar(conditionMessage(e))
)
#> [1] 8190
```

<sup>Created on 2019-08-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

dbplyr can generate very long SQL queries (especially when accessing very wide tables). Some drivers (e.g. SQL Server) include the SQL in the error message, and the cause of the error is stripped and never shown for the user.

Suggesting to split such very long messages halfway and include the first and last 4000 or so characters.

title: Use modulo power of 2 for interrupt checking
description:
Really just a minor thing I noticed, but using a power of 2 instead of 10000 can be significantly faster AFAIK [1]. However this is only relevant for very large datasets.

https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/8cf2858472e849ad73b3485611242ac7dd0c056d/src/odbc_result.cpp#L689-L691

So instead of 10k, one could use 2^13 = 8192 or 2^14 = 16384. I am not entirely sure if the compiler always translates it to a bitwise AND `rows_fetched_ & (8192 - 1)`, but at least there is a chance :) Alternative is to write `if (rows_fetched_ & (8192 - 1) == 0) ...` directly, but this is also less readable.

1: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo_operation#Performance_issues

title: dbExistsTable says table exists when it shouldn't
description:
### Issue and Expected Result
I am trying to drop a table in SQL Server 2017. When I inspect the database, it appears as if the table has disappeared. However, according to odbc, the table still exists. In my example, I am writing a table to a default schema. I then copy the table from default schema into a new table in a new schema. I then drop the table in the default schema. When I run `dbExistsTable()`, it returns TRUE, though.

### Server
SQL Server 2017

### Reproducible Example
```r
dbWriteTable(con, "iris", iris)
dbExecute(con, "SELECT * INTO [schema].iris FROM iris")
dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE iris")

dbExistsTable(con, "iris") # returns TRUE, should be FALSE
dbListTables(con) # iris appears here, it should not appear here
```
### EDIT 1
I will note this error does not appear in the following example leading me to believe something is happening when the table is being copied into another schema.

```r
dbWriteTable(con, "iris", iris)
dbExecute(con, "SELECT * INTO iris2 FROM iris")
dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE iris")

dbExistsTable(con, "iris") # <- returns false as expected
dbListTables(con) # <- iris table does not appear here
```
### EDIT 2
After dropping the newly created table in the non-default schema, the issue is resolved. This behavior, though, is wrong. I should have to specify in dbExistsTable() the schema name to find that the table exists, no?

title: Batches of SQL statements and direct execution
description:
The use case is that I have various templated SQL scripts with multiple statements in each for doing some data loading, cleaning and transformation tasks, where the statements do not return back any data as results. I run such batch queries using `RODBC::sqlQuery(con, query)` with no problem, since this function calls `SQLExecDirect` under the hood. With the DBI interface, I guess, `dbSendStatement` or `dbExecute` would be appropriate functions for that purpose.

However, the only possible way to execute queries in the odbc package is via prepared statements (where it calls `SQLPrepare` and then `SQLExecute`). And the problem is that batch queries cannot be run as prepared statements (at least with Vertica):
```
Error in new_result(connection@ptr, statement) : 
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1344: 42601: ERROR 2446:  Cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement
```
In principle, in order to switch to odbc, I could try parsing my scripts into individual statements and executing those one-by-one. However, it seems wasteful to create and execute hundreds of prepared statement requests, especially when there's no real need for using prepared statements. Also, databases are sometimes set up to auto-adjust user priority when a user is sending too many rapid-fire requests.

Were there any plans to add the direct execution? The nanodbc does offer some methods for that. And I can contribute if there would be interest.

dbWriteTable passing double precision values to DB with single quotes
description:
*@ericbrownaustin commented on Sep 26, 2018, 3:30 PM UTC:*

When trying to write to Hive/Presto DB using dbWriteTable, the function returns an error:

`dbWriteTable(con, name = "db.table", value = dt, overwrite = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)`

```
Error in result_insert_dataframe(rs@ptr, values) : 
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: HY000: [Qubole][Qubole] (50) Query https://us.qubole.com/v2/analyze?command_id=13063516 failed: [2018-09-26T15:19:53.400357 #2507] ERROR -- : Command execution failed with exception: Query 20180926_151953_00448_g8ut7 failed: com.facebook.presto.sql.analyzer.SemanticException
Insert query has mismatched column types: Table: [varchar(255), double, double, double, double, double, double, double, double], Query: [varchar(10), varchar(6), varchar(16), varchar(8), varchar(8), varchar(7), varchar(17), varchar(7), varchar(7)]
com.facebook.presto.sql.analyzer.StatementAnalyzer.visitInsert(StatementAnalyzer.java:258)
com.facebook.presto.sql.analyzer.StatementAnalyzer.visitInsert(StatementAnalyzer.java:166)

```

In looking at the logs, I am seeing the following query passed to the DB:

```
INSERT INTO db.table (columns)
VALUES ('2018-01-01', '206731', '428338.802367312', '19817428', '17092499', '8417922', '0.670020263483696', '1445503', '6972419')
```

The insert query is wrapping each double precision value with single quotes. When resending the same query manually without the quotes around the double precision values, the insert works fine. Is there a parameter that I am not correctly?

title: dbWriteTable() and dbListTables() - missing characters?
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
I am experiencing a weird problem where I try appending to an existing table and I get the response `There is already an object named 'test_table' in the database`.
After doing some digging, I think the problem is in `dbListTables()` and `dbExistsTable()`.

### The code
```
## i built a connection wrapper that works; since querying definitely works...
con <- connect_db()

## everything working fine...
data <- data.frame(a = c(1,2,3), b = c("a", "b", "c"), stringsAsFactors = F)
dbWriteTable(con, "test_table", data, row.names = F)

## this append doesn't work - 
dbWriteTable(con, "test_table", data, append=T, row.names = F)

## Error Message:
Error: <SQL> 'CREATE TABLE "test_table" (
  "a" FLOAT,
  "b" varchar(255)
)
'
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42S01: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server][SQL Server]There is already an object named 'test_table' in the database.

```
Despite the append=T, dbWriteTable is trying to re-create the table. Why? I think because:
`dbExistsTable(con, "test_table")` returns `FALSE`

When I call `dbListTables(con)` I get a really strange response: All the tables are listed with every other character missing. **So `test_table` looks like `ts_al`.**

If we check `dbExistsTable(con, "ts_al")` the return is `TRUE`

I am truly at a loss here, hoping someone has some ideas...
I am using ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server as my driver, and like I said, the connection works. 
Perhaps it is some sort of character encoding issue? I really have no idea...

title: dbGetQuery: Dates as Characters Microsoft SQL
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
`dbGetQuery()` returns character objects instead of date objects from dates on Microsoft SQL Server.

### Database
Microsoft SQL Server (I think 2012)

### Reproducible Example

Example:
```r
library(odbc)
library(DBI)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(drv = odbc::odbc(), dsn = ... , uid = ..., pwd = ...) # Credentials to the Microsoft SQL server.

qry <- "SELECT '2017-01-01' AS date, CAST('2017-01-01' AS date) AS casted_date, CAST('2017-01-01' AS datetime) AS casted_datetime"

date_test <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, qry)


```

This creates the data frame date_test with three columns:
date = Character (should in my understanding be a date object in R)
casted_date = Character (should in my understanding be a date object in R)
casted_datetime = POSIXct (is fine for me)

So, I expected the columns date and casted_date to date objects and not character objects in R.

### Further information

Using RODBC leads to the same result of getting characters instead of dates. Thus, it is possible, that this is some error on my side somewhere in my ODBC settings or on the Microsoft SQL server. I hope that my example above is reproduceable to you in order to rule that case out - or at least limit the likelihood for that. :-)

title: Different behaviour when inserting records using connection with and without Windows Authentication
description:
As per subject.

Using a connection created with `DBI::dbConnect()` with Windows Authentication, `dplyr::db_insert_into()` works as expected, but not when using a connection created with `DBI::dbConnect()` without Windows Authentication (i.e., using user id and password).

Same issue when using `SQL Server Native Client 11.0` and `SQL Server Native Client 13.0` drivers.

``` r
sql_con <- function(dsn = dsn
                    , database = database
                    , UID = UID
                    , PWD = PWD
                    , winauth = TRUE) {
  sql_translate_env.JDBCConnection <<- dbplyr:::`sql_translate_env.Microsoft SQL Server`
  sql_select.JDBCConnection <<- dbplyr:::`sql_select.Microsoft SQL Server`
  
  print(glue::glue("Connecting to: ", database, ".", UID, "@", dsn))
  
  if (winauth) {
    print(glue::glue("Connected to: ", database, ".", UID, "@", dsn))
    # using winauth if dsn
    con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc()
                          ,
                          dsn = dsn
                          , database = database
                          , port = 1433
    )
  } else {
    print(glue::glue("Connected to: ", database, ".", UID, "@", dsn))
    con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc()
                          ,
                          driver = "SQL Server Native Client 11.0"
                          , server = dsn
                          , database = database
                          , UID = UID # rstudioapi::askForPassword("Enter Database user")
                          , PWD = PWD # rstudioapi::askForPassword("Enter Database password")
                          , port = 1433
    )
  }
}

# data to be inserted
output <- readRDS('/output_data/output.rds')

# create connection with winauth = TRUE
con <- sql_con(dsn = "my_dsn"
                            , database = "my_db"
                            , winauth = TRUE)
#> Connecting to: my_db.uid@my_dsn
#> Connected to: my_db.uid@my_dsn


# this works fine; using the connection with winauth = TRUE
dplyr::db_insert_into(con = con
                      , table = "my_table"
                      , values = output
                      , append = TRUE)

# create connection with winauth = FALSE
con_no_winauth <- sql_con(dsn = "my_dsn"
                            , database = "my_db"
                            , uid <- 'my_uid'
                            , pwd <- 'my_pw'
                            , winauth = FALSE)
							
#> Connecting to: my_db.my_uid@my_dsn
#> Connected to: my_db.my_uid@my_dsn

dplyr::db_insert_into(con = con_no_winauth
                      , table = "my_table"
                      , values = output
                      , append = TRUE)
#> Error in result_insert_dataframe(rs@ptr, values): nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42S02: [Microsoft][SQL Server Native Client 11.0][SQL Server]Invalid object name 'my_table'.
```

title: dbWritetable truncates text to 255 characters
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
When writing data to a MSSQL DB using `dbWritetable`, values are truncated to 255 characters. The column type in the database schema is `text`. Manually querying the database from, for example, SQL Server Management Studio with an `INSERT` statement that contains data over 255 characters works fine, meaning the database is not the culprit.

### Database
Microsoft SQL Server 2016 using FreeTDS driver 7.1

### Reproducible Example
```r
library(DBI)
library(odbc)

dbWriteTable(con, table, data, append = TRUE)
```
As a workaround, we're now sending the following query using `dbExecute` instead of using `dbWritetable`, which does not truncate the data:

```
 for(i in seq_len(nrow(data))){
    value_string <- paste(data[i, ], collapse = "', '")
    dbExecute(con, 
              sprintf(paste0("INSERT INTO %s (", paste(dbCols, collapse = ", "), ") VALUES ('%s');"), table, value_string))
```

title: Parameterized Queries Not Working with SQL Server 2017
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
I am trying out parameterized queries on my SQL Server following the documentation provided here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DBI/DBI.pdf. However, it is not working for me. Specifically when I write a query to insert some rows using parameters, the value returned is 0 indicating no rows were affected. In the example I show below, the value should be 2 because 2 rows are going to be affected. Furthermore, when I go to query the entire table, the rows I was supposed to have inserted using parameters do not show up.

EDIT: Looking in the documentation I mention above in the section on parameterizing queries, I noticed SQL Server isn't mentioned. Are parameterized queries available for SQL Server?

### Database
SQL Server 2017

```r
library(DBI)
library(odbc)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

con <- dbConnect(odbc(),
                 Driver = "SQL SERVER",
                 Server = SERVER_NAME,
                 Database = DB_NAME,
                 UID = USERNAME,
                 PWD = PASSWORD)

# Create a table and insert some entries
createTable <- dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE People (id int NOT NULL, name char(10) NOT NULL)")
insertRows <- dbExecute(con, "INSERT INTO People (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Joe'), (2, 'Mark'), (3, 'Laura')")

# The value for insertRowsParams is 0 indicating 0 rows were affected
```

title: SqlServer fails to write records that contain Inf values.
description:
Issue Description and Expected Result
`dbWriteTable` throws an error when trying to write records containing `Inf` values. 

this seems related to #6 and I accept that this may be out of scope. But posting this issue so that other users can find and understand what the following error means.

 ```nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: HY000: The incoming tabular data stream (TDS) remote procedure call (RPC) protocol stream is incorrect. Parameter 1 (""): The supplied value is not a valid instance of data type float. Check the source data for invalid values. An example of an invalid value is data of numeric type with scale greater than precision.,  ```

### Database
Microsoft SQL Server Version: 13.00.5101

Example:
```r
con
#<OdbcConnection> Database@Location
# Database: Database
# Microsoft SQL Server Version: 13.00.5101
dbWriteTable(con, "tmpTestInf", data.frame(y = Inf))
# Error in result_insert_dataframe(rs@ptr, values) : 
```

title: Error converting data type varchar to numeric when writing more than 1024 numeric digits rows to SQL SERVER
SQL Server requires SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON
description:
for proper handling of quotes:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), ...)
DBI::dbExecute(con, "SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON")
```

Otherwise, `"` can't be used to delimit identifiers.

Reference: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/set-quoted-identifier-transact-sql?view=sql-server-2017.

This happens with a connection via FreeTDS, the [reference to `SET ANSI_DEFAULTS ON`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/set-ansi-defaults-transact-sql?view=sql-server-2017) (a superset of `QUOTED_IDENTIFIER`) claims that this is set automatically for ODBC connections.

I wonder if we can/should be issuing this by default for connections to SQL Server, or if this is an upstream issue.

title: DBI::dbExistsTable
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
The `dbExistsTable()` isn't working correctly for me when the table's schema isn't the default.

The  `dbExistsTable()` functions finds the table when I *don't* specify a schema, but not when I do.  In the long term-I'm afraid the wrong table (a 2nd table in a different schema) would be manipulated.

### Database
SQL Server 2016 & 2008

### Reproducible Example

```r
library(magrittr)
table_id <- DBI::Id(
  schema  = "schema_1",
  name    = "car"
)

ds <- mtcars %>% 
  tibble::rownames_to_column("car")

# Create the Table
channel <- DBI::dbConnect(
  drv   = odbc::odbc(),
  dsn   = "cdw_cache"
)
result <- DBI::dbWriteTable(
  conn        = channel,
  name        = table_id,
  value       = ds,
  overwrite   = T,
  append      = F
)

DBI::dbGetQuery(channel, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM schema_1.car")
# Produces `1 32`

# Everything is expected until this line.

DBI::dbExistsTable(channel, table_id)
#Produces: Error in name@name[["table"]] : subscript out of bounds

DBI::dbExistsTable(channel, "schema_1.car")
# Produces: [1] FALSE

DBI::dbExistsTable(channel, "car")
# Produces: [1] TRUE

DBI::dbDisconnect(channel)
```

title: POSIXct losing precision on insert
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

When I insert a `POSIXct` object into the database, it is losing the sub-second precision.

(Code and session info the same as #207)


### Database

```
1> select @@VERSION
2> GO
Microsoft SQL Server 2017 (RTM-CU9-GDR) (KB4293805) - 14.0.3035.2 (X64) 
	Jul  6 2018 18:24:36 
	Copyright (C) 2017 Microsoft Corporation
	Developer Edition (64-bit) on Linux (Ubuntu 16.04.5 LTS)
```

### Reproducible Example

```r
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                   driver='ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server',
                   server='127.0.0.1,31433',
                   database='master',
                   uid='SA', pwd='Mysecretpassword1')

qry <- "create table test1 ( id UNIQUEIDENTIFIER DEFAULT NEWSEQUENTIALID() PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL , f_int INT , f_psx DATETIME, f_psx2 DATETIMEOFFSET )"
data1 <- data.frame(
    f_int  = 1L,
    f_psx  = Sys.time(),
    f_psx2 = Sys.time(),
    stringsAsFactors=FALSE
  )
withr::with_options(list(digits.secs=6), print(data1$f_psx))
# [1] "2018-08-16 23:14:18.559138 UTC"

dbExecute(con, qry)
# [1] 0
dbWriteTable(con, 'test1', data1, create=FALSE, append=TRUE)
a <- dbGetQuery(con, "select * from test1")
withr::with_options(list(digits.secs=6), print(a$f_psx))
# [1] "2018-08-16 23:14:18 UTC"
difftime(data1$f_psx, a$f_psx)
# Time differences in secs
# [1] 0.5591381
```

It's a problem of the insert, since it is being stored with zeroes:

```sql
1> select f_int,f_psx,f_psx2 from test1
2> go
f_int       f_psx                   f_psx2
----------- ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------
          1 2018-08-16 23:14:18.000            2018-08-16 23:14:18.0000000 -07:00
```

title: nvarchar vs ntext in bind
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

String comparisons fail when the column is type `NTEXT`.

This is not a new thing, per se:

title: [FR] be able to control the returned timezone
description:
Hi, first of all, my timezone and my database server's timezone are all Asia/Shanghai (UTC+8).

It's great that we can set the server's timezone info in the odbc connection, a.k.a., `odbc::dbConnect(...,, timezone = 'Asia/Shanghai')`. 

It's also a necessary step to ensure the value uploaded to the server is the same as local. Otherwise, the time will be converted to UTC first before getting uploaded to the server, ending up with a different time value in the server. Moreover, the timezone info get from `DBI::dbGetQuery()` would be UTC which is incorrect either.

Howerver, it causes inconvenient. **The results returned from `DBI::dbGetQuery()` are all converted to UTC timezone and it confuses the users a lot.**

For example, let's say there's a time value `2019-01-01 01:00:00` in the server. The server's timezone is `Asia/Shanghai`. What we get from `DBI::dbGetQuery()` is `2018-12-31 17:00:00 UTC`.

Yes, I know the value it's correct but it's much better if we can simply have the default `Asia/Shanghai` timezone value, a.k.a., `2019-01-01 01:00:00`, by setting somewhere before in the `odbc::dbConnect()`.

**So my proposal is, can we add a new param `timezone_out` in `odbc::dbConnect()` so that we can control the timezone returned from `DBI::dbGetQuery()`?**

Many thanks!

title: Provide fallback implementation to use when parameter binding fails
description: Some databases / drivers have issues with the way nanodbc does parameter binding for inserting data. https://github.com/rstats-db/odbc/issues/66, https://github.com/rstats-db/odbc/issues/30. To work around the issue we can provide a fallback `odbcWriteTableSQL()` function that writes the values as text rather than binding a column. This requires escaping the data specially for things like Dates, datetimes and missing data.

title: dbGet/SendQuery: Dates shifted to day before

I am using the `timezone` argument of `dbConnect()` as the database timezone is set to CET instead of UTC.

title: Feature request: Return data.table from dbGetQuery()
description:
This is a new feature request.

`dbGetQuery()` returns a data frame. The request is to add an option to return a data.table.

I could convert the data frame into a data.table, but this conversion is expensive for large data frames. I want to avoid conversion by having `dbGetQuery()` return a data.table.

```r
library(data.table)
library(dplyr)
library(microbenchmark)

mtcars_small <- mtcars
mtcars_large <- sample_n(mtcars, size=1e6, replace=TRUE)

microbenchmark(as.data.table(mtcars_small),
               as.data.table(mtcars_large),
               times=100)
```

title: Boolean columns are returned as strings
description:
**Steps to reproduce:**
* Open some PostgreSQL connection.
* Run a query that would retrieve a boolean column - e.g.
```R
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "select true as c1")
```
* Inspect resulting `data.frame` in R.

**Expected behavior:** boolean DB results should translate to R logical type (`TRUE`/`FALSE`).

**Actual behavior:** boolean DB results translate to R character type (`"0"`/`"1"`).

Issue is not present with `RPostgreSQL` and `RPostgres`.

title: Handling SQL Server ODBC Connector Error: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server]Invalid Descriptor Index
description:
### Issue

When connecting to a SQL Server Database Table which contains Binary / Encrypted Data (Raw Data), "RODBC" handles it properly, while "odbc" does not:

```{r}
# odbc
r_table <- dbGetQuery(
  con_odbc,
  "
    SELECT TOP 1000
      *
    FROM 
      [Database].[Schema].[Table]
  "
) %>%
  as_tibble()

# RODBC
r_table <- sqlQuery(
  con_RODBC,
  "
    SELECT TOP 1000
      *
    FROM 
      [Database].[Schema].[Table]
  "
) %>%
  as_tibble()
```

With "odbc" Package, the Query fails, but with "RODBC" works.

The difference is that "RODBC" converts Binary Data Columns to Character, and then returns such encrypted columns as:

```{r}
list(as.raw(c(0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00)))
```

Within the data.frame.

title: Feature request: Support for ODBC bulk insert and update operations
description:
I know that the `nanodbc` lib supports bulk inserts and updates via **batch sizes of n rows** that are send to the server via one (or a minimum number of) server roundtrip(s):

https://github.com/lexicalunit/nanodbc/issues/242

Could you support this in the `odbc` package too please?

A simple test with a prepared statement and parameter binding indicates that only one row can be sent but not a whole batch of rows at once (tested with MySQL Version: 5.5.53-MariaDB and an Ubuntu client with unixODBC + DBI_0.5-1 +  odbc_1.0.1):

```
library(DBI)
library(odbc)

con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), dsn="testDB", uid = "user", pwd = "password")

dbWriteTable(con, "iris", iris)      # create and populate a table

# Test bulk inserts
insert <- dbSendQuery(con, "INSERT INTO iris(`Sepal.Length`, `Sepal.Width`, `Petal.Length`, `Petal.Width`, `Species`) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")
dbBind(insert, list(1, 2, 3, 4, "blue"))   # works
dbBind(insert, list(1:2, 2:3, 3:4, 4:5, c("blue", "red")))  # Error: `params` elements can only be of length 1
dbClearResult(insert)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

Bulk inserts and updates are the last missing link for e. g. Microsoft SQL Server since Microsoft does not provide that currently for R even though they have integrated R into the MS SQL Server 2016.

Thanks for this great new package!

title: Compatibility issues of ODBC with R 3.6 (character encoding issues)
description:
# ISSUE
I encountered an issue querying `char` columns from a SQL Server Database in R while running on R 3.6.0 and odbc 1.1.6 on Mac.

There is no issue while running on R 3.3 so I believe it's due to compatibility issues with 3.6.0. 

What happens:
`ODBC` drops even-indexed characters for iso-1 columns.
This dropping of characters is not random: only even characters (2nd, 4th, 6th etc) get dropped.

This is almost certainly due to character encoding.

Look what happens when I run `select @@version` in DataGrip:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40693475/57944832-44760400-78a6-11e9-8e4c-89c28a75018e.png)


vs when I run it in R:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40693475/57944719-dfbaa980-78a5-11e9-999f-adc43da5cb53.png)

The issue is with `CHAR` columns encoded as `iso-1` ( aka Latin-1) but not with columns encoded as `UNICODE`.

title: Large precision numbers not truncated
description:
When I load large precision numbers into the database, the number gets stored improperly. I would expect the large precision numbers to get truncated instead of distorted. For example, `1.1111111111111` might get stored as `1.1111111111123`. See below for a reproducible example on PostgreSQL.

```
library(DBI)
library(odbc)
dd <- data.frame(pi = pi)

con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), "PostgreSQL (DSN)")
dbWriteTable(con, "precision", dd, overwrite = TRUE)
x <- dbReadTable(con, "precision")
sprintf("%.55f", x$pi)
sprintf("%.55f", pi)

#odbc: 3.1415926535897900073734945181058719754219055175781250000
#pi:   3.1415926535897931159979634685441851615905761718750000000
```

Note, this same issue occurs in the `RPostgres` package.

If the query does not include the `text` field `CONTENT`, there's no problem. But if I include it, the query will be hanging forever after fetching 10-30k rows with the following query:

title: datetimeoffset unsupported
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

The SQL Server `DATETIMEOFFSET` field is not recognized and/or formatted correctly. Instead of a "usable" timezone, it's including a rather-verbose version: `"2018-08-16 23:14:18 Pacific Standard Time"`. I can't find it anywhere in the source for `odbc` or `DBI`, though I do find it in the R source [`extra/tzone/registryTZ.c`](https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/15eff2491f650042ddf5485cde247a734799b2e8/src/extra/tzone/registryTZ.c#L95). I know \*this\* one, but I can't assume anything.

I'm not 100% certain this is an `odbc`-thing, frankly, but I am also not where else the problem can be addressed.

### Database

```
1> select @@VERSION
2> GO
Microsoft SQL Server 2017 (RTM-CU9-GDR) (KB4293805) - 14.0.3035.2 (X64) 
	Jul  6 2018 18:24:36 
	Copyright (C) 2017 Microsoft Corporation
	Developer Edition (64-bit) on Linux (Ubuntu 16.04.5 LTS)
```

### Reproducible Example


```r
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                   driver='ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server',
                   server='127.0.0.1,31433',
                   database='master',
                   uid='SA', pwd='Mysecretpassword1')

qry <- "create table test1 ( id UNIQUEIDENTIFIER DEFAULT NEWSEQUENTIALID() PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL , f_int INT , f_psx DATETIME, f_psx2 DATETIMEOFFSET )"
data1 <- data.frame(
    f_int  = 1L,
    f_psx  = Sys.time(),
    f_psx2 = Sys.time(),
    stringsAsFactors=FALSE
  )
withr::with_options(list(digits.secs=6), print(data1$f_psx))
# [1] "2018-08-16 23:14:18.559138 UTC" # currently -7, so 23:14:18 UTC
attr(data1$f_psx, "tz") # to show on TZ assigned yet
# NULL

dbExecute(con, qry)
# [1] 0
dbWriteTable(con, 'test1', data1, create=FALSE, append=TRUE)
str( dbGetQuery(con, "select * from test1") )
# 'data.frame':	1 obs. of  4 variables:
#  $ id    : chr "7DDA423E-F36B-1410-8A8F-007D77BBB095"
#  $ f_int : int 1
#  $ f_psx : POSIXct, format: "2018-08-16 23:14:18"
#  $ f_psx2: chr "2018-08-16 23:14:18 Pacific Standard Time"
```

Most of the `$f_psx2` string is easily parsed into `POSIXt`, but the TZ is confounding me. 

I would be happier with just the character representation from the server, frankly, since that contains a numeric offset and therefore much easier to parse.

For the record:

```r  
Sys.timezone()
# [1] "America/Los_Angeles"
```

This is what the database sees:

```sql
1> select f_int,f_psx,f_psx2 from test1
2> go
f_int       f_psx                   f_psx2
----------- ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------
          1 2018-08-16 23:14:18.000            2018-08-16 23:14:18.0000000 -07:00
```

and similarly, Excel with Microsoft Query:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5815808/44241986-19764c80-a17c-11e8-9543-7d7660685084.png)


So the first column is just a `DATETIME` sans TZ info, which is unacceptable for my use (I could soap-box a long time about databasers who think it's okay to trust clients and programs to always insert times with the same TZ offset).

This doesn't change if R has a TZ attached to the data:

```r
data1$f_int <- 2L
( data1$f_psx <- .POSIXct(data1$f_psx, "US/Pacific") )
# [1] "2018-08-16 16:14:18 PDT"
dbWriteTable(con, 'test1', data1, create=FALSE, append=TRUE)
str( dbGetQuery(con, "select * from test1 where f_int = 2") )
# 'data.frame':	1 obs. of  4 variables:
#  $ id    : chr "80DA423E-F36B-1410-8A8F-007D77BBB095"
#  $ f_int : int 2
#  $ f_psx : POSIXct, format: "2018-08-16 23:14:18"
#  $ f_psx2: chr "2018-08-16 23:14:18 Pacific Standard Time"

data1$f_int <- 3L
( data1$f_psx <- .POSIXct(data1$f_psx, "UTC") )
# [1] "2018-08-16 23:14:18 UTC"
dbWriteTable(con, 'test1', data1, create=FALSE, append=TRUE)
str( dbGetQuery(con, "select * from test1 where f_int = 3") )
# 'data.frame':	1 obs. of  4 variables:
#  $ id    : chr "87DA423E-F36B-1410-8A8F-007D77BBB095"
#  $ f_int : int 3
#  $ f_psx : POSIXct, format: "2018-08-16 23:14:18"
#  $ f_psx2: chr "2018-08-16 23:14:18 Pacific Standard Time"
```

title: Have synonyms show-up for Microsoft SQL Server `dbListTables`
description:
*@brshallo commented on May 7, 2018, 5:21 PM UTC:*

I regularly connect to data marts provisioned for me on Microsoft SQL Server.

When connecting to Microsoft SQL Server, the RStudio "Connections" tab shows "tables" and "views" but does not show "synonyms". ("Synonyms" also do not show-up when running `DBI::dbListTables(con)`)

If I want to view the synonyms in R I will typically do something like:

```
library(tidyverse)
xtypes <- c("V", "SN", "U")
tables_access <- tbl(con, "sysobjects") %>% 
  select(name, xtype) %>% 
  collect() %>%
  filter(str_detect(xtype, "V|SN|U"))

View(tables_access)

```

Though this is less convenient. The ability to connect and query synonyms is unaffected. Only the ability to preview tables via `DBI::dbListTables` / the Connections tab, and only for Microsoft SQL Server.

Right now I end-up usually using Tableau's data previewer in parallel (which I believe is using the same driver but defaults to show synonyms as well as views and tables)...

If it does not make sense to have synonyms show-up by default in the package, do you know what change to options i can make that would make 'synonyms' show-up in my 'Connections' pane in RStudio when connecting to Databases on Microsoft SQL Server?

### System details

```
RStudio Edition : Desktop
RStudio Version :  1.1.282
OS Version      :  Windows 10 Enterprise, x64-based processor
R Version       :  R version 3.4.2 (2017-09-28)

```

### Packages:

```
dbi pacakge version: 0.8
driver: "SQL Server"

```

The same thing occurs whether I'm connecting via windows authentication or with a specific username and password with odbc. The lack of synonyms showing-up when running `DBI::dbListTables` also occurs whether I'm using odbc or RJDBC for connecting.

title: A strange SQL Server + odbc Date error
description:
I'm having a very strange and frustrating error with `Dates` and their underlying `storage.mode()`.

I get data from Bloomberg using the `Rblpapi` package from Dirk. It pushes the data to R from C++ so the problem may lie there. When `Date` objects are pushed up to R from C++, they come in correctly as `Date` objects, but their underling storage mode is `integer`. 

When I try and upload a data frame with an integer storage mode date column, it fails. See below:

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc(),
  driver = "SQL Server",
  Server = "---",
  Database = "---",
  Trusted_Connection = TRUE
)

# Trying to make a Date stored as an integer
my_df <- data.frame(date = as.Date(1L, origin = "1970-01-01"))

# Seems to still be a double though
storage.mode(my_df$date)
#> [1] "double"

# We can force it to be integer (this is how it comes from Rblpapi)
storage.mode(my_df$date) <- "integer"

# There we go
storage.mode(my_df$date)
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(my_df$date)
#> [1] "integer"

# Fails to write (but creates table)
dbWriteTable(con, "##temp_df", my_df)
#> Error in result_insert_dataframe(rs@ptr, values): nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 22007: [Microsoft][ODBC SQL Server Driver][SQL Server]Conversion failed when converting date and/or time from character string.
db_drop_table(con, "##temp_df")
#> [1] 0


storage.mode(my_df$date) <- "double"

# Success!
dbWriteTable(con, "##temp_df", my_df)

# Read in as character?
df <- dbReadTable(con, "##temp_df")
class(df$date)
#> [1] "character"

db_drop_table(con, "##temp_df")
#> [1] 0
```

Hopefully you can reproduce this with a SQL Server instance of your own.

Is this something that should be supported? Maybe `dbWriteTable()` should check that the storage mode is `double` first, but that seems like a hack. Maybe `Rblpapi` should return using the `double` storage mode rather than `integer`.

title: Writing string vector with mixed encodings causes corrupted table contents
description:
I am investigating encoding problems with `odbc` and MS SQL Server (see #56) and can reproduce strange behaviour on **Ubuntu using MySQL (5.7.21 with innodb)** so it is easier to debug without Windows and MS SQL Server.

# Observations

If you write an R character vector with mixed encodings (UTF-8, latin1, ...) into a DB table that was created manually using the correct encoding (UTF8mb4 but also tested with UTF8)...

1. the content of the table is displayed incorrectly (e. g. using a DB frontend like MySQL Workbench 6.5.2.0)
2. the content is read back incorrectly
3. while entering a UTF-8 text directly into the table does display the correct string in the MySQL Workbench

**Side note**: If `dbWriteTable` creates the DB table the data can be read back to R correctly (= same bytes) but is still displayed incorrectly in the DB table!

A related issue may be: #143

# Steps to reproduce the problem

Install MySQL using docker (if not already present): `docker pull mysql`

Start MySQL with:

```
docker run --name DBImysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=my_secret -e MYSQL_DATABASE=testdb -p 30001:3306 -d mysql
```

Then use this R script:

```
library(DBI)
# library(odbc)   # devtools::install_github("r-dbi/odbc")

# test data taken from package DBItest:
# https://github.com/r-dbi/DBItest/blob/master/R/utf8.R
text_cyrillic <- "\u041a\u0438\u0440\u0438\u043b\u043b"
text_latin <- "M\u00fcller"
text_latin_encoded <- iconv(text_latin, from = "UTF-8", to = "latin1")
text_chinese <- "\u6211\u662f\u8c01"
text_ascii <- iconv("ASCII", to = "ASCII")

mixed_enc <- c(text_cyrillic, text_latin, text_latin_encoded, text_chinese, text_ascii)

data <- data.frame(ID = 1:length(mixed_enc),
                   mixed_enc = mixed_enc,
                   enc = Encoding(mixed_enc),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

#   ID mixed_enc     enc
# 1  1    Кирилл   UTF-8
# 2  2    Müller   UTF-8
# 3  3    Müller  latin1
# 4  4    我是谁   UTF-8
# 5  5     ASCII unknown

# ensure pre-condition
stopifnot( Encoding(mixed_enc) == c("UTF-8", "UTF-8", "latin1", "UTF-8", "unknown"))

con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc()
                 , .connection_string = "driver=MySQL;server=127.0.0.1;port=30001;user=root;password=my_secret;database=testdb;option=3;protocol=tcp"
                 , encoding = "UTF-8") # utf8mb4 didn't work neither (if encoding should mean "connection character set")

table_name <- "encoding_test"
if (dbExistsTable(con, table_name)) { dbRemoveTable(con, table_name) }
# trying utf8 instead utf8mb4 does not help and is not recommended, see:
# https://medium.com/@adamhooper/in-mysql-never-use-utf8-use-utf8mb4-11761243e434
sql <- paste0("CREATE TABLE ", table_name, "(ID int, mixed_enc varchar(255) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4, enc varchar(255))")
dbGetQuery(con, sql)

# nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42000: [MySQL][ODBC 5.1 Driver][mysqld-5.7.21]SET NAMES not allowed by driver
# dbGetQuery(con, "SET NAMES utf8;") # communicate with the server using the utf8 character set

dbWriteTable(con, table_name, data, overwrite = FALSE, append = TRUE)

# dbWriteTable(con, table_name, data, overwrite = TRUE)
# Note: Using overwrite = TRUE creates the wrong CHARACTER SET for the mixed_enc column (causing corrupted characters)
#       but reading back the rows re-creates the same strings again in R (this is still not correct since
#       the database content is corrupted). dbWriteTable creates this table:
# CREATE TABLE `encoding_test` (
#   `ID` int(11) DEFAULT NULL,
#   `mixed_enc` text,
#   `enc` text
# ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=latin1;

res <- dbReadTable(con, table_name)
dbDisconnect(con)

res$res_enc <- Encoding(res$mixed_enc)

print(res)     # for debugging
#   ID      mixed_enc     enc res_enc
# 1  1   ÐšÐ¸Ñ€Ð¸Ð»Ð»   UTF-8   UTF-8
# 2  2        MÃ¼ller   UTF-8   UTF-8
# 3  3        MÃ¼ller  latin1   UTF-8
# 4  4 æˆ‘æ˜¯è°\u0081   UTF-8   UTF-8
# 5  5          ASCII unknown unknown

# SELECT * FROM testdb.encoding_test;
#
#   ID      mixed_enc     enc
#    1   ÐšÐ¸Ñ€Ð¸Ð»Ð»   UTF-8
#    2        MÃ¼ller   UTF-8
#    3        MÃ¼ller  latin1
#    4 æˆ‘æ˜¯è°\u0081   UTF-8
#    5          ASCII unknown
```

title: Managing of Scheduled R script
description:
I scheduled the Rscript which takes data from MS SQL Server and performs regression. The script takes only new data.
For example, today was loaded 100 obs from 01.01.2017-03.03.2017,script conducted the regression on this data.

Tomorrow will be loaded 100 obs from 04.03.2017-04.06.2017 and script will work with this obs and not from 01.01.2017 -04.06.2017.

I asked at this forum the question,how to make that R only works with data that have a fresh date and got this useful answer,
where we create last date log and take the data older than it.
If anyone is interested, here the link
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/50275618/create-sql-expression-in-r-for-certain-condition

    # READ DATE FROM LOG FILE
    log_dt <- readLines("/path/to/SQL_MaxDate.txt", warn=FALSE)
    
    # QUERY WITH WHERE CLAUSE
    sql <- paste0("SELECT Dt, CustomerName, ItemRelation, SaleCount, 
                          DocumentNum, DocumentYear, IsPromo
                   FROM dbo.mytable WHERE Dt > '", log_dt, "'")
    
    df <- sqlQuery(dbHandle, sql)
    
    # RETRIEVE MAX DATE VALUE
    max_DT <- as.character(max(df$Dt))
    
    # ...here code for regression, now, it's not important for this question
    
    # WRITE DATE TO LOG FILE
    cat(max_DT, file="/path/to/SQL_MaxDate.txt")

The question:My Scheduler runs 1 time per day, but it happens that the data in the SQL database does not load every day, it can loaded for example 1 time of 3 days and so on. 
Can R make a check?
If R determines that there is no new data( there is no fresh date), then the script does not start?
If R  determines("see") that there is new data, it runs script.
I.E. for example, last date when Rscript ran ,was 12.05.2018, and 13.05.2018 Rscipt was run by schedule, but  on this date nothing was loaded in sql, R "see" that there is no new date, and it will work with same last date and it doesn't run. And R must do this checking everytime when running, is there new date or not.
Is it possible to do or no?

title: odbc doing very odd things with dates
description:
### Demo

Differing Date return behavior based on machine. 

On certain machines, for the same query, we get different data types for identical versions of odbc and driver.

And while I understand that not everyone deserves a date, and that some have to rely on the strength of their character, this is getting nutty.

For the purpose of this example, I used two Macs with apparently identical operating systems, both of which install R via homebrew. But my test set included several windows users on windows 10 and 7 and ubuntu 16.04

It is possible that there is some dependent C library that is different between them. This is actually my operating assumption about this issue.


Illustration of issue:

I had several people run this same code:
```r
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), 'XXXXXXX', 
                               uid = getOption('ODBCuid'), 
                              pwd = getOption('ODBCpwd'),

out <- dbGetQuery(con, 'select top 1 Date from olap.vdimdates')
print(out)
```

My driver reports as `SQL Server Version: 15.7.0`, though the full specification in `/etc/odbcinst.ini` is:

I can use this driver successfully with `RODBC`, and with `DBI` + `odbc` as long as all the columns in the result set are some numeric variant.

title: can't copy_to schema other than Dflt.
description:
I am using dbplyr and odbc to connect to a "Microsoft SQL Server" database running Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise version 12.0.5556.0.  When I run

```r
# db previously defined as an odbc/Microsoft SQL Server connection
service.tbl <- c('A' = 'Army', 'N' = 'Navy', 'M' = 'Marine Corps', 'F' = 'Air Force') %>%
               data_frame(ABBR = names(.), SERVICE = .)
service <- copy_to(db, service.tbl, in_schema('MAP', 'SERVICE'), temporary=FALSE)
```
I get the error:
```
Error: <SQL> 'SELECT *
FROM MAP.SERVICE as 'zzz1'
WHERE (0 = 1)'
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42S02: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 11 for SQL Server][SQL Server]Invalid object name 'SERVICE'.
```

However the table was created just in the wrong place.
```r
DBI::dbListTables(DB) %>% grep('SERVICE', ., value=TRUE)
```
produces
```
[1] "MAP.SERVICE"
```
Also
```r
tbl(db, in_schema('MAP', 'SERVICE'))
```
fails. Whereas,
```r
tbl(db, in_schema('Dflt', '[MAP.SERVICE]'))
```
does not and gives the correct contents of the table.

I traced this down to the DBI::dbCreateTable,OdbcConnection,character,data.frame-method which in turn calls the dbQuoteIdentifier method.  at this point the `in_schema('MAP', 'SERVICE') is evaluated as the character string MAP.SERVICE with the classes `c('ident_q', 'ident', 'character')` and the ident classes are disregarded and the table name becomes '"MAP.SERVICE"' with the double quotes which is the wrong thing to do.  This could be remedied by defining a method for `dbQuoteIdentifier`.

```r
setMethod(dbQuoteIdentifier, list(conn = 'Microsoft SQL Server', x= 'ident'),
function(conn, x, ...){
    return(DBI::SQL(x))
}
```

This fixes the problem for me.  There might be more issues related to it but there does need to be some more consideration for database schemas.

*NOTE:* I apologize for not having a reproducible example that can be run directly, but the database I work with is behind several layers of firewall.

title: "internal SAVEPOINT failed" on travis
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
With PostgreSQL and when using `dbExecute()` to set a SAVEPOINT or release it, I get the error `nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: HY000: internal SAVEPOINT failed ` when querying data from the database. Strangely, I cannot reproduce this locally but only on [travis](https://travis-ci.org/sebschub/klimageodb/builds/314707309) and only with a table defined before. 

This might be an issue with some old odbc package or driver on Travis and not an issue with the odbc R package. Please feel free to close this if it is the case. It might be related to #118.

### Database
PostgreSQL v9.6 on travis

### Reproducible Example

[Travis is set-up](https://github.com/sebschub/klimageodb/blob/travis/.travis.yml) and [one table is created](https://github.com/sebschub/klimageodb/blob/travis/travis/create_tables.sql). The issue is only with this table, not with the `testtable` created below. The code

```r
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), dsn = "klimageodb")

dbWriteTable(con, "testtable", data.frame(a=10, b=20))

dbBegin(con)

dbExecute(con, "SAVEPOINT testSP;")
cat("First table 1 before\n")
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM testtable;")
cat("First table 1 after\n")
dbExecute(con, "RELEASE SAVEPOINT testSP;")

dbExecute(con, "SAVEPOINT testSP;")
cat("First table 2 before\n")
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM testtable;")
cat("First table 2 after\n")
dbExecute(con, "RELEASE SAVEPOINT testSP;")

dbExecute(con, "SAVEPOINT testSP;")
cat("Second table 1 before\n")
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM site;")
cat("Second table 1 after\n")
dbExecute(con, "RELEASE SAVEPOINT testSP;")

dbExecute(con, "SAVEPOINT testSP;")
cat("Second table 2 before\n")
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM site;")
cat("Second table 2 after\n")
dbExecute(con, "RELEASE SAVEPOINT testSP;")

dbCommit(con)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

produces the error

```
  First table 1 before
  First table 1 after
  First table 2 before
  First table 2 after
  Second table 1 before
  Error: <SQL> 'SELECT * FROM site;'
    nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: HY000: internal SAVEPOINT failed 
```

title: MSSQL Connection Description
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

In the readme part connecting to MS SQL or SQL Server is not represented properly. After checking `odbcinst.ini` you can find the proper driver name. The latest driver name for Linux is "ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server". You can add the code below.  Many other sources use "SQL Server" only which returns driver not found error.

<!--Example: `dbGetQuery()` returns incorrect timestamps.-->

### Database
SQL Server on Linux

### Reproducible Example

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                      driver = "ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server",
                      server = "<SERVER_IP_OR_localhost>",
                      database = "<YOUR_DB_NAME>",
                      uid = "<YOUR_DB_USER_ID>",
                      pwd = "<YOUR_DB_USER_PASS>")
```

title: odbc returns double quotes for empty IDENT
description:
When using an aggregate function in `dplyr` without a group, the `GROUP BY`  clause is being operated as: `GROUP BY ""`, this causes an error. I was able to track down the issue to an empty IDENT being interpreted as an empty character, thus returning the double quote:

```
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dbplyr)
  library(dplyr)
  library(RSQLite)
  library(DBI)
})

con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), Driver = "SQL Server", Server = "localhost\\SQLEXPRESS", 
  Database = "datawarehouse", Trusted_Connection = "True")

empty <- ident(as.character())
empty
#> <IDENT> [empty]

DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, empty)
#> <SQL> ""

dbDisconnect(con)
```

The issue seems to be in the `dbQuoteIdentifier` method.  A simple fix should be to skip quoting if `x` is 0 length.

A PR is forthcoming for this.

title: R session corrupts if ODBC connection doesn't return a data.frame
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

As you know, `ODBC` is not always used to connect a database, there're data services provide API via ODBC connection. We send correponding query command to the connection and it returns the data. 

However, if the api thinks the query command is invalid or it can't be returned as a data.frame, it returns a character error message.

It works fine on `RODBC` because `RODBC` simply return the error message to R. 

In the contrast, `odbc` will try to parse the character error message to a `data.frame` and it leads to the corruption of the R session.

The expected result is an R error message. It should not leads to the corruption of R sessions.

### Database
The data service is [Tinysoft](http://www.tinysoft.com.cn). I'm afraid that you can't reproduce since it's not for free.

### Reproducible Example
As mentioned above, the api is not free, so you can't reproduce it. 

#### works fine in RODBC
```r
sql <- "setsysparam(pn_stock(), 'SZ000002'); return close();"
rodbc_conn <- RODBC::odbcConnect("Tinysoft")
RODBC::sqlQuery(rodbc_conn, sql, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# [1] "S1000 -1 General error---Execute: unsupported return type"                                    
# [2] "[RODBC] ERROR: Could not SQLExecDirect 'setsysparam(pn_stock(), 'SZ000002'); return close();'"
```

#### R session corrupts in odbc
```r
conn <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), "Tinysoft", encoding = "GB2312")
DBI::dbGetQuery(conn, sql)
```

title: dbDisconnect doesn't always close the connection after a committed transaction
description:
I'm having an issue with transactions in `odbc` and closing the connection afterwards. Please let me know if there's something I'm missing. Thanks.

### Issue Description and Expected Result
<!--Example: `dbGetQuery()` returns incorrect timestamps.-->
If an explicit transaction is started with `odbc::dbBegin`, and then committed with `odbc::dbCommit`, then `odbc::dbDisconnect` does not appear to actually close the connection with the database. 

If you try to call `dbDisconnect` a second time, the "Connection already closed" warning message appears, `dbIsValid` is `FALSE`, and the entry for that connection does disappear from the RStudio "Connections" pane, but the connection does not appear to be actually closed at the database. For example, DB2 will list that connection as still open with the "db2 list applications" command, and Access will not delete its lock file (*.laccdb). Restarting R seems to close the connection.

The behavior is the same whether or not any actual work is done within the transaction. If work is done, committing does seem to work (changes are visible in the DB). If the transaction is cancelled with `dbRollback` instead, the subsequent `dbDisconnect` appears to work correctly.

I'm more interested in getting it to work with DB2, but I had tried Access as well to see if it was driver/database-specific. I would try others but I don't have any other drivers installed.

### Database
<!--Example: PostgreSQL 9.5, SQL Server 2012-->
IBM DB2 LUW 10.5.1, MS Access 2016

### Reproducible Example
Since the unwanted behavior is visible even when no work is done in the transaction, no specific table definitions or data should be required. I use a blank, brand new Access database file below, which seemed the easiest.

```r
cstr <- "Driver={Microsoft Access Driver (*.mdb, *.accdb)};Dbq=C:/blank_database.accdb;"
conn <- odbc::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), .connection_string = cstr)

odbc::dbBegin(conn)
odbc::dbCommit(conn)

odbc::dbDisconnect(conn)
```

title: Cannot overwrite or append in schemas
description:
### Description
It seems that specifying a schema using `DBI::SQL()` prevents the use of `overwrite` and `append`. Here's an example using the `public` schema, but obviously it is when using other schemas that it is hard to work around.

### Database
PostgreSQL 9.3.20 64-bit

### Example
``` r
library(DBI)                                                                       
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), driver = "PostgreSQL Unicode", database = "odbc")
                                                                                   
dbWriteTable(con, "a", data.frame(a=1, b=2))                                       
dbWriteTable(con, "a", data.frame(a=1, b=2))                                       
#> Error: Table a exists in database, and both overwrite and append are FALSE
dbWriteTable(con, "a", data.frame(a=1, b=2), overwrite = TRUE)                     
dbWriteTable(con, "a", data.frame(a=1, b=2), append = TRUE)                        
                                                                                   
dbWriteTable(con, DBI::SQL("a"), data.frame(a=1, b=2))                             
#> Error: Table a exists in database, and both overwrite and append are FALSE
dbWriteTable(con, DBI::SQL("a"), data.frame(a=1, b=2), overwrite = TRUE)           
#> Note: method with signature 'DBIConnection#SQL' chosen for function 'dbQuoteIdentifier',
#>  target signature 'PostgreSQL#SQL'.
#>  "OdbcConnection#character" would also be valid
dbWriteTable(con, DBI::SQL("a"), data.frame(a=1, b=2), append = TRUE)              
                                                                                   
dbWriteTable(con, DBI::SQL("public.a"), data.frame(a=1, b=2))                      
#> Error: <SQL> 'CREATE TABLE public.a (
#>   "a" DOUBLE PRECISION,
#>   "b" DOUBLE PRECISION
#> )
#> '
#>   nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42P07: ERROR: relation "a" already exists;
#> Error while executing the query
dbWriteTable(con, DBI::SQL("public.a"), data.frame(a=1, b=2), overwrite = TRUE)    
#> Error: <SQL> 'CREATE TABLE public.a (
#>   "a" DOUBLE PRECISION,
#>   "b" DOUBLE PRECISION
#> )
#> '
#>   nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42P07: ERROR: relation "a" already exists;
#> Error while executing the query
```

title: Encoding problem with dbWriteTable on Microsoft SQL Server 2012 with R on Windows7 client
description:

When I write a latin1 string into a `nvarchar` column of a table the text written into the database table
is wrong:

```
1 façile

2 Ã€Ã¶ÃŒÃ
```

```
col1
faÃ§ile
Ã€Ã¶ÃŒÃ
aaa
```

title: dbBegin() after dbRollback(): "Double begin" with PostgreSQL
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
After a transaction has been started with `dbBegin()` and stopped with `dbRollback()`, I cannot start a new transaction with `dbBegin()`; it produces the error "Error in connection_begin(conn@ptr): Double begin". Stopping a transaction with `dbCommit()` and starting a new one with `dbBegin()` is fine. While the documentation says that "nested transactions are not supported by DBI, an attempt to call dbBegin() twice yields an error", I don't think that a `dbBegin()` after `dbRollback()` is a nested transaction. Testing it with the command line tool `psql` works without any issues.

RPostgreSQL does not produce this behaviour, thus, I would suspect the reason in the odbc package.

### Database
PostgreSQL 9.6.4 on openSUSE 42.3. "PSQLtest" in the example is just a very simple entry in the odbc.ini.

### Reproducible Example
``` r
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), "PSQLtest")

dbBegin(con)
dbCommit(con)
dbBegin(con)
dbRollback(con)
dbBegin(con)
#> Error in connection_begin(conn@ptr): Double begin
dbRollback(con)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

title: SQL Server - NA_integer_ stored as -2147483648

title: Issues with SQL Server Spatial function STAsText()
description:
I guess this won't be a particularly mainstream issue, but I have the need to extract data from SQL Server Spatial databases on Linux, and using the official Microsoft ODBC driver.  This driver cannot be used to extract geography types without truncating them (the Windows driver works fine), but I was hopeful of being able to extract geographies as WKT using the STAsText() function.  When I do this, however, I generally get an error.  As an example:

```r
library(DBI)
library(odbc)

con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), 
                 Driver = "SQL Server",
                 Server = "192.168.20.21",
                 Port = 1433,
                 Database  = "gis",
                 Schema = "geography",
                 UID = "gisuser",
                 PWD = "password")

shp <- dbGetQuery(con, "select f_geometry_column from dbo.geometry_columns where f_table_name = 'mb2013'")[1,1]
cols <- dbListFields(con, "mb2013")
query <- sprintf("select top 10 %s, %s.STAsText() as WKT from geography.mb2013",
                 paste(cols, collapse = ", "),
                 shp)

res <- dbGetQuery(con, query)
```

produces the error:

```as.is
Error in result_fetch(res@ptr, n, ...) : 
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:2834: 07009: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for S
```

Curiously, it sometimes works.  For example, the following query works:

```as.is
select top 10 ogr_fid, mb2013, ogr_geometry.STAsText() WKT from geography.mb2013
```

but this doesn't (same query, but columns in a different order):

```as.is
select top 10 ogr_fid, ogr_geometry.STAsText() as WKT, mb2013 from geography.mb2013
```

It produces a slightly different error, though (different line number):

```as.is
Error in result_fetch(res@ptr, n, ...) : 
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:2890: 07009: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for S
```

I get the similar errors on Windows, but again with different numbers `nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:xxxx`.

Note that this all works if I switch to using the `RJDBC` package with the official MS JDBC driver, but for various reasons I'm trying to avoid a solution which uses the JVM... plus I just really like this `odbc` package and how easily I can use it with `dbplyr`, for example.

Anyway, I appreciate that this might be hard to reproduce, or reproducing it might take a bit of work, but thought I'd ask the question anyway.

title: installation fails with compilers that don't understand `-std=c++11`
description:
It looks like the C++ standard used during compilation of `cctz` is hard-coded here as `c++11`:

https://github.com/rstats-db/odbc/blob/12a44e1b3447a388df283ee97aa02c3393e0d7cf/src/cctz/Makefile#L24

Is there any chance this could be relaxed to `c++0x`, for older compilers that implement the subset of C++11 features required for this library? Or are relatively modern compilers required here?

title: Options for mapping BIGINT
description:
In Vertica, all integer types are synonyms for the same signed 64-bit BIGINT. With the change in #9 to use the bit64's integer64 type to represent such numbers, all my integer columns are now pulled as integer64. In general, I tend to use integer64 only when really necessary, and to stay away from using them for computations as much as possible b/c of hidden quirks such as
```R
> mean(1:2L)
[1] 1.5
> mean(as.integer64(1:2L))
integer64
[1] 1
```
That is, integer64 is not a drop-in replacement for integers.

Would it be possible to have a global configuration option for how BIGINT is mapped? E.g.:
- "integer64" (default)
- "integer" coerce to integer (user must be aware of possible consequences)
- "numeric" coerce to double

title: Provide workaround for `SQLTable(tableType = "LOCAL TEMPORARY")`
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
`SQLTable(tableType = "LOCAL TEMPORARY")` and `SQLTable(tableType = "GLOBAL TEMPORARY")` are supposed to return local and temporary tables regardless of dbms system. However it seems very few drivers implement this functionality.

In order to work around this issue we can define a new generics `odbcListLocalTemporaryTables()` and `odbcListGlobalTemporaryTables()` with methods various dbms methods.

We can also provide a default method that queries SQLTable() with `tableType = LOCAL TEMPORARY` and `GLOBAL_TEMPORARY`, although as I have not seen that functionality actually implemented in any drivers.

title: dbWriteTable adds quote marks to an SQL Server query which causes a permission error
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
dbWriteTable returns permission error when writing to a specific DB and Schema on SQL Server (12.0.5).

I am trying to write to a database where I have read/write/edit permissions on a specific schema however when using dbWriteTable the query generated is trying to write to the master database instead.

I believe it's because the query generated has quotes around the table name:

`CREATE TABLE "[DB].[SCHEMA].[TABLE]" (`

If I use the same code directly in SQL Server Studio but without the quotation marks the table is created successfully.

I have tried installing and using different ODBC Drivers however each one ends with the same permission error.

Is this something I'm doing wrong or an issue in the package?

### Database
SQL Server (12.0.5)

### Reproducible Example
Example:
```r
  con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
```

title: dbConnect() not working with the 1.1.1 CRAN update
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

`dbConnect()` not working anymore with the 1.1.1 CRAN update. Incomprehensible error. Potentially an error in the package install process.

### Database

Microsoft Access Version 14.0. 

I don't know if Access is fully supported yet (from what I can tell, no), but the connection worked yesterday before the CRAN update, and I was able to pull data using `dbGetQuery()`.

To prove that the information is correct, here is a working connection to RODBC.

title: Fetching GUID data type columns gives a warning
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
If an SQL Server data base contains a GUID field, `dbReadTable(db, "tablename")` (and similar commands) issue warnings like this:

    Warning message:
    In result_fetch(res@ptr, n, ...) : Unknown field type (-11) in column guid

However, the field is read as a string, and works perfectly fine.

### Database
```r
> dbGetInfo(db)
$dbms.name
[1] "Microsoft SQL Server"

$db.version
[1] "11.00.6020"
```

### Additional information
There is some information about the data type at https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/uniqueidentifier-transact-sql
And more information on the various ODBC SQL data types at https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/appendixes/appendix-d-data-types. According to that document ,the GUID data type has the ODBC SQL data type name `SQL_GUID` (numeric identifier: `-11`).

Treating the value as a string should be OK, so the only thing that needs to be done to ‘fix’ this bug is to make the warning go away. :)

title: dbplyr with odbc::odbc(): Truncated error messages
description:
Hi,

I'm using dplyr/dbplyr from Linux with kerberos authentication to access a SQL Server 2016 database.

### Issue Description and Expected Result
Interaction with the database via standard dplyr verbs seem to be working fine, but a few operations seem to give errors, like writing tables to the database and printing them to the console (yet View()ing works fine). However, those errors are truncated so I don't actually get the substance of the message.

I don't have a reprex as I'm unable to create a public-facing database. I have pasted my code and the errors below:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)
library(DBI)

con_odbc <- dbConnect( 
  odbc::odbc(),  #don't need to load the odbc package, it's only called here
  .connection_string = paste0("driver=SQL Server Native Client 11.0;", 
                              "server=servername.junkdomain.local;", 
                              "database=AbTables;", 
                              "trusted_connection=yes;") 
)

copy_to(con_odbc, nycflights13::flights, "flights",
        temporary = FALSE,
        indexes = list(
          c("year", "month", "day"),
          "carrier",
          "tailnum",
          "dest"
        )
)
```
Expected result would be a successful copy of the table to the database.  Note I have no troubles copying the data over using `dbWriteTable(con, 'flights', nycflights13::flights)` from DBI. Instead, I get:

As you can see it's truncated. At first I thought it said: "Cannot find the covfefe" but that was just my imagination. :) Note that I don't have any trouble uploading the table using the dbWriteTable() function from DBI

Any tips on how I might dig under the hood and get the full error message so I can file a more useful issue would be appreciated.

title: Cannot set transaction isolation level in SQL Server
description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result

When I execute a `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED` query on a SQL Server database, it doesn't change the [isolation level](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/develop-app/transaction-isolation-levels). That can be determined with a `SELECT transaction_isolation_level FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions where session_id = @@SPID` query. Setting this transaction level is necessary for production databases so that queries from R don't lock out other queries.

### Database

Microsoft SQL Server, both 2012 (see below) and 2016.

### Reproducible Example

Here's an example on the sample AdventureWorks2012 database (though I get the same problem on our own database, running SQL Server 2016).

``` r
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                 driver = "libtdsodbc.so",
                 database = "AdventureWorks2012",
                 uid = "sqlfamily",
                 pwd = "sqlf@m1ly",
                 Server = "mhknbn2kdz.database.windows.net",
                 port = 1433)

# First check the transaction level
s <- "SELECT transaction_isolation_level FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions where session_id = @@SPID"
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, s)
#>   transaction_isolation_level
#> 1                           2

# This should change it to 1
q <- "SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED"
set_result <- DBI::dbExecute(con, q)

# But it does not:
s <- "SELECT transaction_isolation_level FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions where session_id = @@SPID"
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, s)
#>   transaction_isolation_level
#> 1                           2
```

description:
### Issue Description and Expected Result
<!--Example: `dbGetQuery()` returns incorrect timestamps.-->
Data imported into R from MS SQL Server shows local time zone.  But wrong time.  The time is off by the offset between UTC and local time zone.

### Database
<!--Example: PostgreSQL 9.5, SQL Server 2012-->

Client computer MS Windows 7 latest patches

   $nickname

R Studio 1.0.143.

### Reproducible Example
> library(tidyverse)
> library(lubridate)

> Sys.timezone()
[1] "America/New_York"

>con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                     driver = "{SQL Server Native Client 11.0}",
                     server = "myserver",
                     database = "mydatabase",
                     Trusted_Connection = "yes")

> orders <-
      con %>% 
         dbReadTable("my_table") %>%
         head

> orders$order_dt
[1] "2003-06-18 05:05:40 EDT" "2003-06-18 05:16:45 EDT"
[3] "2003-06-18 05:20:46 EDT" "2003-06-18 05:30:58 EDT"
[5] "2003-06-18 05:27:38 EDT" "2003-06-18 05:37:06 EDT"

However, these times are 4-5 hours earlier in the day then when SSMS reports the same times depending on the time of year.

I took a look at some of the code.  (I;m new to R but no expert.) But, it looks like odbc may be expecting to get UTC data.  However, my SQL server is giving you "America/NewYork".  You are recording the value as UTC.  Then when R is displaying the value, it is showing me the values in local time zone.  (4-5 hours earlier)

I've tried to figure out if there is a way to have the odbc driver show time zones so that R can interpret my data more accurately.  No luck I've tried 
> orders$order_dt_only <- with_tz(orders$order_dt_only, tz = "UTC")
But now the time is in UTC.  But, the event actually occurs local time.  And, I'd prefer not to re-load every variable that happens to be a data time.

Dates and time are important for the work I'm doing.  If there is a workaround, that would be very helpful.  Or a tidyvers type suggestion that would allow me to work with this data in an easier way.

Thanks for any insights.  

</details>

select queries are faster with the RODBC package on Hadoop databases
description:
### Impala/Hive queries faster when using RODBC
This isn't a bug per say. However I've noticed that  `dbGetQuery()` type queries are consistently slower on Hadoop (at least on our installation).

### Database
Cloudera Impala CDH 5.7.1 and Cloudera Hive CDH 5.7..1

### Reproducible Example

I cannot produce a fully reproducible example since to my knowledege DBI doesn't provide standard Hive/Impala tables that can be tested with minimal work. I can say however that I have seen substantial (up to 3x times faster) on select queries using a Teradata database when using `odbc` in place of `RODBC`. Maybe there's something particular in how Hive/impala queries are handled that's not reflected in `odbc`'s current implementation.

Example:
```r
library(RODBC)
library(microbenchmark)
library(odbc)

conn_impala <- odbcConnect("ODBC-Impala-XXXX")
conn_impala_dbi <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), "ODBC-Impala-XXXX")
query_impala <- "select * from database.logs where part_date = '2016-12-15' limit 1000000"
microbenchmark(
  odbc = res_odbc_impala <- dbGetQuery(conn = conn_impala_dbi, query_impala),
  rodbc = res_RODBC_impala <- sqlQuery(channel = conn_impala, query_impala),
  times = 1L
)

  expr      min       lq     mean   median       uq      max neval
  odbc 403.3625 403.3625 403.3625 403.3625 403.3625 403.3625     1
 rodbc 152.5502 152.5502 152.5502 152.5502 152.5502 152.5502     1
```

title: Handling of dates
description:
I realize that this project may be under develpment, but I thought I would try it out.  
With a small amount of testing I found it to work well, but I noticed that plain SQL dates (on SQL Server) seem to be handled wrong.  Below is a quick example illustrating the example.  I would be happy to provide more details if you like.

```
library(odbconnect)
conn <- dbConnect(odbconnect::odbconnect(), 
                  driver = "{SQL server Native Client 11.0}", 
                  Server = "MYSERVER\\MyInstance", 
                  Trusted_Connection = 'yes')

R <- dbSendQuery(conn, "select cast('2015-1-1' as date) d1, cast('2015-1-2' as date) d2, cast('2015-1-1' as datetime) dt")
X <- dbFetch(R)
stopifnot(dbClearResult(R)) # ok
stopifnot(class(X$d1) == 'Date', class(X$d2) == 'Date', class(X$dt) == c("POSIXct", "POSIXt" )) # ok
stopifnot(identical(as.POSIXct('2015-1-1', tz='UTC'), X$dt)) # ok
stopifnot(format(X$d1) == "3053957-01-18") # passes, but surprising!

dbDisconnect(conn)
```

Thanks for your work on this so far.
